en: Now, therefore, he offers the Śatarudriya oblation.
Herein this entire Agni has been consecrated; he is here the deity Rudra, into whom the gods have placed this immortal, supreme form. He is here shining brightly.
"Standing and eating, he was seeking food; therefore, the gods were afraid of him, thinking, 'Lest he should harm us.
They said, 'Let us prepare food for him; with that we shall appease him. For him they prepared this food, the *cāntadevatya*; with it they appeased him. Now, as to this..."
He pacified the god with this; therefore, it has the pacifying deity as its presiding deity.
They call that the *śatarudriya* cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. In the same way, he bestows upon him this immortal, supreme form; this very [rite] is here.
He stands glowing, desiring food; for him he prepares this food, which has the pacified deities as its divinity;
by that he pacifies him.
He offers with *jartila* seeds.

As he is being piled, he is born; he is born for the sake of all food. Now, both of these are food: the wild sesame seeds and that which is domestic. Insofar as they are sesame seeds, they are domestic;
insofar as they ripen on unploughed ground, they are wild. Thus, with both kinds of food, he gratifies him—the domestic and the wild.
And with a leaf of the *arka* tree he offers.
The *arka* is food; verily, by means of food he thus gratifies him.
He offers in the enclosing stones;
for these enclosing stones are Agni. Thus, his oblations become offered as if they were in Agni itself.
Furthermore, as to why he offers this Cāturmāsya oblation to Rudra:

when Prajāpati had become relaxed, the deities departed from him; only one deity did not abandon him—namely Wrath (Manyu). He stood there stretched out across the unbroken space; he wept, and those which were his tears...
They leaped into that fury and settled within it; he himself became Rudra with a hundred heads and a thousand eyes, possessing a quiver of a hundred arrows.
And those other drops that fell became innumerable thousands who entered these worlds. Because they wept (*arudan*), they are called *rudrās*; thus, this very one is Rudra with a hundred heads.
The thousand-eyed one, with a hundred quivers, his bow strung, standing ready to strike and terrifying [all], stood there desiring food; therefore, the gods were afraid.
They said to Prajāpati:
"We are indeed afraid of him, lest he should harm us," they said.

He replied, "Prepare food for him; with that, appease him. For him they prepared this food, the *Catarudriya*; with it they appeased him. Now, as to why [this is performed] for those of a hundred heads...

They pacified Rudra with this; therefore, because they pacified Rudra of the hundred heads with this, it is called the *caturudriya*. Indeed, that which pacifies Rudra of the hundred heads is what they call the *caturudriya* cryptically (*parokṣa*), for the gods love the cryptic. In the same way, for him...
He prepares this food, the Śatarudriya; by means of it, he pacifies him.
He offers oblations of Gavedhuka-grain flour.
For from the place where that deity lay shattered, Gavedhuka-grains arose.
They came into being; thus he gratifies him with his own portion, with his own essence.
He offers with an *arka* leaf;
for the *arka* tree exists through the desire of this very deity.
He thus gratifies him with his own portion, with his own essence.
He offers in the enclosures (*pariśrit*);
for the enclosures are indeed the body hairs, and there is neither poison nor anything else in the body hairs.
Standing facing north, he offers in the northern half of the fire; for in this direction lie the abodes of this deity.
Thus he gratifies him in his own quarter and sacrifices to him in his own quarter.
He first utters "svāhā" at the height of the knee.
That which is knee-high is, as it were, below; and this world is, as it were, below. Thus, he gratifies those Rudras who entered this world. 9.1.1 [12].
Then, at the height of the navel.
That which is navel-high is indeed like the middle;
the intermediate region (antarikṣaloka) is like the middle. Thus he gratifies those Rudras who entered the intermediate region.
Then [the one] mouth-high.
That which reaches to the mouth is, as it were, above; and that world yonder is, as it were, above.
Thus he gratifies those Rudras who entered that world with the utterance *svāhā*. The *svāhā* is indeed food; verily, by means of food he gratifies them. 9.1.1 [14]
"Salutation to thee, O Rudra, for thy wrath"— for that wrath which was extended and remained within him,
to that he thus offers salutation; "and also salutation to thy arrow, and salutation to thy two arms"— for indeed, [it was] both by the arrow and by the two arms.
And he remained there, striking terror [into all].
9.1.1.[15] He is this divine Kṣatriya; he who became possessed of a hundred heads is the Kṣatriya, while these others who arose from the drops are the Viś (the common people).

The subjects became equal to this ruling power (kṣatra); therefore, these subjects offered up this first portion (uddhāra) for it—namely, this first Anuvāka—and thereby gratified it. In the same way, this [priest] now offers up this first portion for it and thereby gratifies it. Therefore, this [Anuvāka] is dedicated to a single deity, Rudra.
For by this he indeed gratifies him.
These sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) are fourteen in number;
thirteen months are a year, and Prajāpati is the fourteenth.

Agni is Prajāpati; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just so much food does he thus gratify him. "Homage, homage!"—homage is indeed the sacrifice; with the sacrifice, with this act of homage, he pays him reverence. Therefore, one should not say of that which is unfit for sacrifice, "Homage to you!"; for it would be just as if one were to say of him, "The sacrifice to you! 9.1.1. [17]

Then he offers to the pairs, saying, "Homage to so-and-so and to so-and-so. This is just as if one were to say, "May both you and this person not harm me"; for indeed, one who is known and addressed does not cause harm. 9.1.1. [18]

"Obeisance to Hiraṇyabāhu, the leader of the army, and obeisance to the Lord of the quarters. He who is Hiraṇyabāhu is indeed this [Agni], he is the leader of the army, he is the Lord of the quarters. Therefore, whatever here has a single deity, by that he gratifies him alone—the nobility itself.

He makes a share for the Viś; therefore, whatever belongs to the Viś, the Kṣatriya has a share in it. Now, those thousands that were innumerable and entered these worlds—those are the deities to whom he offers this oblation.
Then he offers to those who have been born.

These Rudras entered these creatures wherever they were; it is there that he now gratifies them. Moreover, these are the lineages of the Rudras among the gods, and humans follow the pattern of the gods; therefore, these are the lineages of humans. Thus, he gratifies them according to their very birth. 9.1.1 [20]

Of these, some pay homage on both sides, while others pay homage on only one side; those who pay homage on both sides are indeed more terrible and less peaceful. It is precisely on both sides that he [protects] them with this sacrifice and this act of homage.
He pacifies [the fire].
He indeed offers with "svāhā" at every eighty [verses]:
in the first section (*anuvāka*), then at every eighty, and then at every eighty—whatever [verses there are].
The *yajus* formulas are directed upwards, while the food-offerings are directed downwards; by means of food, he thus gratifies them.
Then he mutters these *yajus* formulas:
"Homage to you, the Kirikas"—this is indeed his most celebrated abode.

Just as a beloved son or one's own heart, so is this deity; therefore, whenever one has any apprehension regarding this deity, one should offer oblations with these *vyāhṛtis*. Thus one indeed approaches the beloved abode of that deity, and so this deity does not harm him. 9.1.1 [23]

"Obeisance to you, the Kirikas"—for these indeed perform all this; "to the hearts of the gods"—these are Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya, for these are the hearts of the gods; "obeisance to the Vicinvatkas"—for these indeed [perform] this...
"Salutation to those who investigate all; salutation to those who destroy," for these indeed destroy him whom they wish to destroy.
"Salutation to those who have not been driven out," for these have not been driven out from these worlds. 9.1.1 [24] Then he mutters the subsequent verses.

"O Drāpi, Lord of the Soma-juice!"—for he is indeed Drāpi; he causes that one whom he wishes to cause to flee to flee. "Lord of the juice"—that is, "Lord of the Soma. "O Daridra, O Nīlalohita"—these are his names and these are his forms;
by mentioning his names, he thus gratifies him. "Of these progeny, of these cattle... [mā...].
"Bhermā roṅno ca naḥ kiṃ canāmamat" (May there be no fear for us, nor anything that may afflict us)—as the *yajus* is, so is its explanation (*bandhu*).
9.1.1. [25] This is the divine Kṣatra;
for this Kṣatra, these subjects [offer] that...

They extracted the *uddhāra* (extra portion) from the front—that which was the first *anuvāka*; then they extracted this *uddhāra* for him from above, and thereby gratified him. In the same way, this one extracts this *uddhāra* for him from above, and thereby gratifies him; therefore, this [offering] also belongs to a single deity.
It becomes indeed fierce, for he thus gratifies him with this.
There are seven of these sacrificial formulas (*yajus*).
The fire-altar consists of seven layers; there are seven seasons; the year is the year.
As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just so much food he thus gratifies him.
Those two sets together amount to twenty-one: twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first; it is for the sake of this correspondence. 9.1.1 [27]
Then he offers the *avatāna* oblations.
For the gods, having gratified them with this food, then unstrung their bows with these *avatāna* offerings; in the same way, this sacrificer now [does so] for these [Asuras] with this food.
Having pleased them, he then strings their bows with these unstrung cords; for with a bow that is not unstrung, one does not strike anyone.
"That [distance], indeed, is a thousand yojanas," so it is said.
This indeed is the furthest distance: that which is a thousand *yojanas*.
That which is the furthest distance—that very thing he unstrings these bows.
Furthermore, as to why he says "a thousand *yojanas*": [it is because]...

"This fire [reaches] a thousand *yojanas*; for there is nothing else beyond it, neither more nor less. Therefore, when one offers an oblation into the fire, one thereby unstrings their bows at a distance of a thousand *yojanas*. There are thousands beyond counting."
"In this great ocean"— wherever those [waters] are,
there he unstrings these bows for them.
He offers these ten unstrung [oblations].
The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; Agni is the *virāj*. There are ten directions; the directions are Agni. There are ten vital breaths (*prāṇas*);
the vital breaths are Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thereby unstrings their bows.
9.1.1 [32] Then he offers the oblations of descent.

This very [sacrifice], rising upwards from here, ascends these worlds; it rises as if turning away. This earth, indeed, is the foundation. Those gods returned toward this foundation; in the same way, the sacrificer now returns toward this foundation. 9.1.1. [33]
Moreover, when he descends again, he follows after these [fires], thus pleasing them; from that very point he withdraws himself for the sake of life.
Thus, with this self, he attains a full span of life.
Moreover, as to why he descends again:
it is indeed these Rudras whom he gratifies here from above; them he then [gratifies] again from beyond, directed hitherward. 9.1.1.[35]
"Let there be homage to the Rudras who are in heaven"—by this he pays homage to those Rudras who are in yonder world.
"Whose rain is their arrows"—for rain is indeed their arrows; by means of rain they strike down whomever [they wish].
"May they not harm us" (9.1.1.36). "Homage be to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space"—
this refers to those Rudras who are in the world of the intermediate space.

He pays homage to them with the words, "Homage to those whose arrows are the wind"; for their arrows are indeed the wind, and by means of the wind they strike down whomever they intend to harm. 9.1.1 [37]. "Homage be to the Rudras who are upon the earth."

Thus, he pays homage to those Rudras who are in this world, with the words, "To those whose food is arrows. Indeed, food is their arrows; for by means of food they strike down whomever they wish to harm. To them [he offers] ten [stalks] facing eastward.

"Ten to the south, ten to the west, ten to the north, ten upwards"—the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Agni is the Virāj; there are ten directions, and Agni is the directions; there are ten vital breaths, and Agni is the vital breaths. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much food does he thus gratify them. 9.1.1 [39]
And as to why he says "ten by ten":
there are ten fingers on the hands; thus, in every direction, he makes this salutation with joined palms (*añjali*) to them.
Therefore, being afraid of them, he makes this salutation, saying, "Let there be homage to them!"—thus he pays homage to them for our sake.
"May they be gracious," he says; thus they indeed become gracious to him. "Whom we hate and whoever hates us—him we place in their jaws," he says;

whomsoever he hates and whoever hates him, him he places in their jaws. He should say, "I place so-and-so in their jaws" regarding the one he hates; then, indeed, there is no longer anything left in that person. Yet, one should not pay heed to this.
For he himself has designated him whom one who knows this hates. (9.1.1 [40]) He descends three times;
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is.

By this much he satisfies them with food; for the *svāhā*-utterance is indeed food, so it is with food that he thus satisfies them. He ascends three times; that makes six, the significance of which has been explained. Furthermore, as to why he descends three times.
For he rises upwards three times; as many times as he rises upwards, so many times does he descend again.
Then he throws that *arka* leaf into the *catvāla* pit.
Verily, by this he performs this rite belonging to Rudra;
it is unappeased. He hides it away so that no one may stand over this unappeased thing, lest it should injure him. Therefore, at the *cātvāla*; for indeed, the fire is this very *cātvāla*.
And as for the *yaccātvāla*, this fire indeed burns it up.
Now, therefore, follows the calculation. Regarding this, they say: "How does this *Caturudriya* attain the year-long Agni?
How is it made to correspond with the year-long Agni? There are indeed sixty and three hundred [verses] in this *Caturudriya*. And—

Now, those which are thirty, or thirty-five, or sixty and three hundred, are as many days as there are in a year; he thus obtains the days of that year. And those which are thirty are the nights of a month; he thus obtains the nights of that month.
Thus he obtains both the days and nights of the year. Now, as for those which are thirty-five...

The thirteenth month is the self; the thirty-fold is the foundation; the two vital breaths and the two [eyes] are the head—thus it is thirty-five. So great indeed is the year. In this way, he attains this *Caturudriya* as Agni the Year; in this way, he becomes one with Agni the Year. Such is the case in the *Śāṇḍila* fire-altar.
In the middle of the fire, the *yajuṣmatī* bricks are laid down; for these bricks are indeed separate fires.

Thus, these fires of his become separately offered with the *Śatarudriya*. Regarding this, they say: "How does he attain this *Śatarudriya* as the Great Litany (*mahaduktha*), and how [does it become] the Great Litany?"
It is accomplished thus: those twenty-five *yajus* verses on both sides of the eighty [verses] constitute the twenty-five-fold self (*ātman*).

Where there is the self, that indeed is the head, and those are the wings and the tail. Now, as for the eighty [verses], that is the attainment of the eighties, for by means of the eighties the Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*) is proclaimed. Then, as for what is beyond the eighty, that is what was previously mentioned regarding the Great [Hymn].
Beyond eighty [verses] of the *uktha*, this is its [portion]; thus indeed he attains this great *uktha* of the *Caturudriya*, and it is thus completed with the great *uktha*. 9.1.2.
Then he sprinkles him from here around.
Having appeased him with the Śatarudriya, the gods then appeased him further; in the same way, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya, he now appeases him further. 9.1.2. [2]
He sprinkles it all around with water.

Water is indeed a means of pacification; he thus pacifies it. He sprinkles it all around on every side; he thus pacifies it on every side. He sprinkles it three times; Agni is threefold—whatever the extent of Agni, whatever his measure is.
By this much alone he thus appeases him. Furthermore, as to why he sprinkles around it: this Agni is indeed these worlds; he thus encloses these worlds with water.

The ocean encircles them on all sides; therefore, the ocean flows around these worlds on every side. Moving to the right, it flows around these worlds to the right. 9.1.2 [4] He sprinkles water around the fires.

This Āgnīdhra is Agni; for one does not injure oneself by oneself, so it is for the sake of non-injury. From stone [he takes water], for from stone waters arise; from the armpit [he takes water], for from the armpit waters arise;
from the right armpit [he takes water], for from the right armpit waters arise. 9.1.2. [5]
"In the rock, in the mountain, the strength that has taken refuge"— for this strength is indeed rested upon the rock, in the mountains, namely the waters;
"the milk gathered from the waters, from the plants, and from the trees," for it is indeed from all of these that it has been gathered.
"O Maruts, bestowing favor upon us, grant us this gathered milk, this food, and this strength"—for the Maruts indeed rule over the rain.

"May hunger be in the stone," he says; thus he places hunger in the stone, and therefore the stone is not eaten. Moreover, the stone is firm, and hunger is firm; thus he places that which is firm into that which is firm within himself.

He takes it up with "Strength!"—he thus places strength within himself. In the same way a second time, and in the same way a third time. (9.1.2) Having set down the fire-remover, he turns around three times; for this indeed makes him lighter, as it were, when he has been encompassed on all sides.
He moves around it; thus he makes amends to it for the sake of non-injury.
And as to why he turns back:
this [earth], indeed, follows after him; therefore, he withdraws himself from it.
"May he live; thus indeed, by means of this self, he attains a full lifespan. (9.1.2[8]) He turns over three times;
for he goes around three times, and as many times as he goes around, so many times does he turn over. (9.1.2[9])
Then, having placed that stone in a carrying-basket, they carry it toward this direction; for this is the quarter of Nirṛti;
thus he places the impurity in the very quarter belonging to Nirṛti. 9.1.2.[10]
The gods,

having appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, then removed his heat and evil by means of this [offering]; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now appeases him with the Śatarudriya and with water.
Having thus pacified it, he thereby drives away its sorrow and evil.
He carries the fire outside;
for this fire is indeed these worlds, and he thus places the sorrow outside of those worlds.
This altar is indeed outside the altar; thus he places the pain outside of it.
Standing facing east on the southern hip of the altar, he throws [the clod] out toward the south, saying: "Him whom we hate—him I cast to you."
"Let its heat reach him whom we hate"—this is what he says. "Let its heat reach so-and-so"—he should say this of the one whom he hates;

then indeed it does not return to him again. Yet one should not pay heed to this, for he whom one who knows this hates is already pointed out by himself. If [the vessel] should not break, he should say, "Let it break"; for when it breaks, then [the enemy] is broken.
He approaches that which he hates; they come upon it without waiting, and thus they leave behind that evil. 9.1.2.
[13] He returns and makes the bricks into milch-cows.
Indeed, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, the gods [did this].
Having struck away his pain and evil, they returned and made the bricks into milch-cows;
in the same way, this [sacrificer], having appeased him with the *Catarudriya* and with water, and having struck away his pain and evil, returns and makes the bricks into milch-cows. 9.1.2. [14]
"One should perform it while sitting," so say some, for "one milks a cow while sitting. But one should indeed perform it while standing;
for this fire-altar is these worlds, and these worlds are, as it were, standing; moreover, one who stands is more vigorous. 9.1.2 [15]
Standing facing north or east—this cow stands facing west before the sacrificer; for they approach the cow standing from the south, facing west. 9.1.2 [16]
Wherever he reaches [the end], having touched that, he mutters this sacrificial formula: "O Agni, may these bricks of mine be milch-cows.
For Agni alone has power over the making of these into milch-cows; therefore, for so many [bricks]...

The gods addressed Agni alone, saying: "One and ten, and the end, and the highest number. Now, that which consists of one and ten is the lower limit of abundance; but this, the end and the highest number, is the highest limit of abundance. Having thus encompassed them from the lower limit and from the highest limit, the gods made them into milch-cows.
In this very way, having grasped them from both the lower half and the upper half, he makes them milch-cows;

therefore, one need not even take care to make many of them. For here on earth, by means of the *brahman* and the *yajus*, he makes them many; but when he connects them in succession, it is desires alone that he thereby connects. 9.1.2. [17]
Furthermore, as to why he makes the bricks into milch-cows:

this Agni is indeed speech, for he is built up by means of speech. When he says, "One and ten, and the end and the beyond-end," it is because one is speech, ten is speech, the end is speech, and the beyond-end is speech; thus, the gods [bestowed] speech itself upon him.

In the same way, the sacrificer makes speech itself a cow; and when he connects [the verses], he thereby connects speech. "O Agni, may these bricks of mine be cows for me in yonder world, in that world"—it is thus that he makes them cows in this world, and then he makes them cows in yonder world.

In this same way, these [waters] enjoy him in both worlds, in this one and in that one. "O seasons!"— for these are indeed the seasons— "increasers of the season (ṛtāvṛdhaḥ)"— that is to say, "increasers of truth"— "you are in the seasons, O increasers of the season."
"Thus, either the days and nights are the bricks, or the days and nights abide within the seasons; [with the words] 'dropping ghee, dropping honey,' he thus makes them drop ghee and drop honey.
"They are called Virājs."

The gods indeed invoked these bricks by their names; as they called them each one, those [names] turned back toward them. Then the *lokampṛṇā* bricks stood facing away, having no assigned names and being prone to fall down. They gave them the name "Virāj," and they turned back toward them. Therefore, there are ten bricks for each [section].

Having placed [the bricks], he consecrates them with the *lokampṛṇā* formula; thereby he makes them the *virāj*. For the *virāj* consists of ten syllables and is a cow of plenty that is never exhausted; thus he makes them cows of plenty that are never exhausted. 9.1.2.
[20] Then he draws a line across them.

With a frog, with an *avakā* plant, and with a branch of reed— having thus appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, and having struck away his heat and his evil, the gods then appeased him further; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, strikes away his heat.
He strikes away evil, and then he pacifies him even further; he draws him apart from all sides and thus pacifies him from every side.
Furthermore, as to why he draws him apart:
Now, when the Rishis, the vital breaths, first prepared this Agni, they sprinkled him with water; that water spilled over and became frogs.
They said to Prajapati:
"What indeed has gone down from us as our desire? he asked.

"This tree knows," he replied. "Let him know; let him fully know. They call that *vetasa* (cane) by name cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. And because they said, "Downward has our desire gone," they became the *avākās*, the downward-flowing ones.

They call them "avakās" cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic; these are indeed the three kinds of water—namely, the frog, the avakā plant, and the reed-shoot—and with these three waters he thus pacifies him.
Furthermore, as to why he draws him across.
He is born when he is built up; he is born for the sake of all food.
Indeed, all this is food: the frog, the avakā plant, and the branch of the vetasa reed, for these are cattle, waters, and trees.
Verily, with all this food he gratifies him. 9.1.2. [24]
By means of the frog, [he wins] cattle;

therefore, the frog is the least fit for the subsistence of cattle, for it is exhausted. By means of the *avakā* plant, [he wins] water; therefore, the *avakā* is the least fit for the subsistence of water, for it is exhausted. By means of the reed (*vetasa*), [he wins] water.
Therefore, among the trees, the cane is the least fit for human subsistence, for it is exhausted [of sap].
Having tied those [stalks] together on a bamboo pole,
he drags them eastward between the enclosing stones on the southern side of the fire-altar.
"With the *avakā* plant of the ocean, O Agni, we encircle you; be purifying and auspicious for us"—this means "we pacify you with the waters of the ocean. 9.1.2 [26].
Then, he sprinkles water with the rear half [of the vessel].

"With the caul of the cold we envelop thee, O Agni; be purifying and auspicious unto us"—for that which is the extreme cold of the cold is the caul of the cold; "with the extreme cold of the cold we appease thee," so it means. 9.1.2 [27]
Then, with the second half [of the verse], he first [performs the rite] as follows:

"Approach the earth, approach the reed; descend into the rivers, O Agni! You are the bile of the waters; come hither with those [waters], O female frog! And make this sacrifice of ours auspicious, O you of purifying color. Just so...
The *yajus* and its significance are thus [9.1.2.28].
Now, with the eastern half, he pours [the water] toward the south:
"This is the gathering-place of the waters, the dwelling of the ocean; [I take] these others for you..."
"May their weapons burn us; may Pāvaka be auspicious for us"—as the *yajus* formula is, so is the binding.
First he draws [the furrow] toward himself; then thus, then thus, then thus; that is turned to the right, for that is the way among the gods.
He first draws it toward himself.
For the self indeed arises first for one being born, then the right wing, then the tail, then the left; that is a clockwise movement, for such is the way among the gods.
He draws the wings and the tail toward himself.

He bestows peace upon himself from the front toward the rear; he thus bestows peace from the further side toward this side. With "O Agni, the Purifier, with thy light," he [lays down] the right wing; with "O Purifier, shining for us," the tail; and with "By the purifying, observant, and gracious [flame]," the left wing.
"Purifier, purifier"—for that which is auspicious and tranquil is indeed the purifier; he thus pacifies it.
He draws [the furrow] with seven [verses].
The fire-altar consists of seven layers; there are seven seasons in the year; the year is...
"As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he draws him apart. He should throw that bamboo pole onto the rubbish heap (utkara).
Then he sings around it with Sāmans.
At this point, this entire Agni has been consecrated; therein the gods placed this immortality."
They bestowed this supreme form upon him; likewise, he now bestows this immortal, supreme form upon it.

The *sāmans* are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); the vital breaths are indeed immortality. Thus, he bestows this immortal, supreme form upon it. He sings around it on all sides; verily, he bestows this immortal, supreme form upon it from every side. 9.1.2 [33]
Furthermore, as to why he sings around him with Sāmans:
the gods indeed desired, "May we make this self of ours boneless and immortal. They said, "Discern that [means]!"
"Let us make this self boneless and immortal," they said. "Reflect upon it!
they said; by this they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)," for they were saying, "Seek [a way] so that we may make this self boneless and immortal.
As they were reflecting and perceiving these commonalities, they sang around him with them;
by means of those [chants], they made this self boneless and immortal. In the very same way, the sacrificer [does so].
When he sings around him with the *sāman*s, he thereby makes this very self boneless and immortal.
He sings around it on all sides; thus he makes this very self boneless and immortal on every side.

He sings while standing, for these worlds are, as it were, standing; moreover, one who stands is indeed more powerful. Having uttered the *hiṅ* sound, he sings, for in that [sound] everything is contained.
The *sāman* becomes complete.
9.1.2.[35] He sings the *gāyatra* first.
The *gāyatra* is indeed Agni; he thus makes this [the sacrificer’s] head Agni; moreover, it is the head.
Thus he makes this boneless, immortal for him.
On the right wing is the *rathantara*;
this earth is indeed the *rathantara*, for it is the most essential among these worlds.

"In this [earth], indeed, are all these flavors; for they call that *rathantara* the 'most flavorful' (*rasatama*) cryptically, since the gods desire the cryptic. He thus makes this earth its right wing; moreover, he thereby makes its right wing boneless and immortal. 9.1.2 [37]
The *bṛhat* is on the left wing.
The *bṛhat* is indeed heaven, for heaven is the highest; he thus makes heaven its left wing.
Moreover, he thereby makes that left wing boneless and immortal. 9.1.2 [38]
The Vāmadevya is the self.
The Vāmadevya is indeed breath, and breath is wind. Wind is the self of all these gods; he thus makes wind his own self. Moreover—
He thus makes his own self boneless and immortal.
The *yajñāyajñiya* is the tail;
for the *yajñāyajñiya* is indeed the moon, since whatever sacrifice is completed [ends with it].
This indeed is the essence of those oblations that he attains; and because this sacrifice after sacrifice attains him, therefore the moon is [called] *yajñāyajñiya*.
He thus makes the moon his tail; moreover, he makes for him this boneless, immortal tail. 9.1.2. [40]
Then he sings the Heart of Prajāpati.
Yonder sun, indeed, is the heart; it is smooth, for the heart is smooth;
it is circular, for the heart is circular; he sings it in the self, for the heart is in the self.

He sings [the verse] "In every armpit, for the heart is in the right armpit; from there the heart is closer"—thereby he makes the sun itself his heart; moreover, he thereby makes his very heart boneless and immortal.
He sings concerning both offspring and Prajāpati.
In that he sings among the creatures, he places the heart in the creatures;
and in that he sings in Prajāpati, he places the heart in Agni.
Furthermore, in that he sings both among the creatures and in Prajāpati—
This Agni is both the creatures and Prajāpati;
thus, when he sings over the fire, he places the heart within both the creatures and Prajāpati.
These, indeed, are the immortal bricks.
He lays down the *tāūttamā* bricks; he thereby places immortality as the highest thing for this entire universe.

Therefore, immortality is the highest thing for this entire universe. No one other than the *adhvaryu* should sing [the *sāman*]; for these bricks are indeed the *iṣṭakās*, and he would be pierced through were anyone other than the *adhvaryu* to sing. 9.2.1. [1]
On the day of the Upavasatha, when the sun has risen in the morning, he releases his speech. Having released his speech, he takes five-fold drawn clarified butter;
into that he throws five pieces of gold. Then this triad becomes poured together: curds, ... [and] ... .
He places honey and ghee in a vessel, a pot, or a large bowl, and puts a handful of *darbha* grass upon it. Then he ascends the fire with the mantra:
"Homage to your heat, to your flame; homage be to your radiance. At this point, this entire fire [is present].

He has been consecrated here; therefore, it is enough [to say], "that which one might injure, that which one intends to injure. For whomever he injures, he injures him either with his heat (*haras*), or with his glow (*śocis*), or with his flame (*arcis*). Thus, he does not injure him with these. "May your missiles burn others than us; may you, O Purifier, be auspicious unto us"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*). 9.2.1. [3]
Having ascended the fire, he pours clarified butter over the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
He pours it with fivefold-drawn butter; the significance of this has already been explained.
He pours it over the *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
The *svayamātṛṇā* brick is the vital breath; he thus places that food in the vital breath.
Furthermore, as to why he pours butter over the *svayamātṛṇā*: this [brick] is the high altar (*uttaravedi*) of Agni; now, as for that former [altar]—
He sprinkles [the ghee] transversely; for this is the sacrificial essence of the Adhvara, and it belongs to Agni—this he now sprinkles transversely.
While looking at it, he sprinkles gold there;
for that which one sees is manifest, and manifest indeed is [the sacrifice].
In this case, they are indeed already strewn with the high altar (uttaravedi); for that which is strewn is cryptically referred to as the high altar, and this [earth] is cryptically the high altar.
He sprinkles it with the utterance "svāhā."
The *svāhā*-utterance is indeed manifest, and the *uttaravedi* is manifest; the *veṭ*-utterance is beyond the eye, and this *uttaravedi* is beyond the eye.
With clarified butter they sprinkle the *uttaravedi*, for it is with clarified butter that they pour out over the *uttaravedi*—with [clarified butter] taken five times.
For they sprinkle the high altar with fivefold-seized butter, alternatingly; for they sprinkle the high altar alternatingly.
"To the one sitting among men, vauṣaṭ! [he says].

The *nṛṣat* is indeed the vital breath; "men" (*naraḥ*) are human beings. Thus, he gratifies that fire which is this vital breath within human beings with the words, "To him who sits in the waters, veḍ! He thereby gratifies that fire which is in the waters. With the words, "To him who sits on the sacrificial grass, veḍ! he gratifies that fire which is in the plants. With the words, "To him who sits in the forest, veḍ! he gratifies that fire which is in the trees.
"To Svarvid, Veḍ!"—this Agni is indeed the Svarvit; he thus gratifies this very Agni.

And as to why he says, "To Nṛṣad, Veḍ! To Ap-sad, Veḍ!"—these are the names of this very Agni; he thus gratifies them. He makes them a deity by means of the oblation; for she alone is a deity for whom an oblation is taken, and not she for whom it is not.
Moreover, he thus places these very fires into this fire by mentioning their names.
He offers these five oblations;
the fire-altar consists of five layers, there are five seasons, and the year is the year.
"As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food does he thus cause him to breathe.
Then he sprinkles him with curds, honey, and ghee; for he is born when he is built up. He is this very one.
It is born for all food; for this curd, honey, and ghee are indeed all food.
He thus gratifies it with all food. He sprinkles it from all sides;
he thus gratifies it from all sides with all food. 9.2.1. [12]
And as to why he sprinkles him:
here this entire Agni has been consecrated; therein the gods bestowed this supreme form upon him, and in the same way, this [sacrificer] bestows that supreme form upon him. Food, indeed, is...
This is the supreme food, namely curds, honey, and ghee; that which is the supreme form, that he places within this [brick] as the highest.
He sprinkles it all over, even from the outside, though it is enclosed on all sides; thus he places this supreme form within it on every side.
He does so with *darbha* grass, for they are pure and fit for sacrifice; with their tips, for the tip is the foremost.
[Regarding the verse] "Of the gods" (devānām) 9.2.1.[13]: Furthermore,
as for why he sprinkles him [the fire],
it is because at the very beginning, when the *ṛṣi*s— those vital breaths (*prāṇa*)— first [established] this Agni...
They consecrated him; they made that [milk] his fore-share.

Then, when he was piled up, they made this [curds] his upper share. Therefore, when he sprinkles with curds, he gratifies those very vital breaths, the seers, who, when he was piled up, made this their upper share. He does so with curds.
"With honey and ghee"— its etymological explanation has been stated [above]. "Those gods who are of the gods,
the worthy of sacrifice who are of those worthy of sacrifice"— for these are indeed the gods among gods, and the most worthy of sacrifice among those worthy of sacrifice.

“They have partaken of their yearly portion,” for they indeed wait upon this yearly portion; “they who eat the oblation at this sacrifice,” for the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed non-eaters of the offered oblation; “let them themselves drink of the honey and the ghee,” that is to say, let them themselves drink of both the honey and the ghee. 9.2.1 [15]
"Those gods who attained godhead among the gods"— for these are indeed the gods who attained godhead among the gods;
"those who are the precursors of this Brahman"— this Agni is the Brahman, and they are his precursors, without whom [the Soma] does not flow clear.

"Is there any abode?"—"No, indeed; apart from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), there is no abode whatsoever. "Neither on the ridge of heaven nor on the earth"—this means neither in heaven nor on earth, but wherever there is a bearer of life, in that [it is]. (9.2.1) He sprinkles [the horse] with two verses.
The sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus sprinkles him. 9.2.1.
[17] Then he descends.

"Bestowers of out-breath, bestowers of in-breath"—for all these are indeed the vital breaths of this built-up fire-altar. If one were not to utter here this self-consecration formula, then this [altar] would surely seize his vital breaths;
but because he utters here this self-consecration formula, it does not seize his vital breaths: "Bestowers of out-breath, bestowers of in-breath."
"Bestowing breath, bestowing luster, bestowing wide space"—this he says; "Thou art a giver to me," this is what he means to say. "May thy missiles burn others than us;
be thou purifying and auspicious for us"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*).
Having returned, he proceeds with the *pravargya* and the *upasad* rites.

Having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, he then gives him either the vow-food (vrata) or the half-vow-food (vārḍhavrata). Then, having again performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, he finally sets aside the Pravargya vessel, having attained that desire for which he performed the Pravargya. 9.2.1 [19]
One should indeed cause it to subside in a pool.
For it becomes heated and glowing;
if one were to cause it to subside in this earth, its heat would enter this earth; if one were to cause it to subside in water, its heat would enter the water. But—
That which flows around [the fire] sweeps away [impurities]; thus he does not harm the waters, nor does he harm this earth.

Because he does not throw [the fire] into the waters, he does not harm the waters; and because the waters flow all around it, and since water is a means of pacification (*śānti*), he does not harm this earth.
Therefore, he should extinguish [the fire] by letting it flow around. 9.2.1. [20]
But rather, one should set it down in the fire.
For this fire is these worlds, and the enclosing stones are the waters; when he sets it down in the fire, he thereby sets it down in the flowing waters. 9.2.1 [21]
Moreover, as to why he deposits [the Pravargya vessels] upon the fire:

this fire is indeed these worlds—Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya—and these are the Pravargyas. If he were to deposit them elsewhere than on the fire, he would thereby place those deities outside of these worlds; but when he does so on the fire...
He thus drives away these very gods and establishes them in these worlds.
Furthermore, as to why he sets it aside on the fire-altar:
the Pravargya is the head of the sacrifice, and this piled fire-altar is the body.
If he were to set it aside elsewhere than on the fire, he would place the head outside of him; but since he sets it aside on the fire, having thus prepared his very self, he restores the head to it.
He sets aside the first *pravargya* vessel so that it is touched by the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.

The *svayamātṛṇā* brick is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the *pravargya* is the head; this built fire-altar is the body. Thus, he connects and joins the head and the body by means of the vital breath.
Having removed the *pravargya*, [he does so] according to its removal. 9.2.2. [1]
Having returned and being about to cast the fire [into the hearth],
he offers oblations and lays on fuel-sticks; for it was with these very oblations and fuel-sticks that the gods gratified him from the front as he was approaching.

In this very way, as he approaches from the front, he gratifies him with food, with oblations, and with fuel-sticks. He takes [the ghee] in five ladlings; the significance of that has been explained. Then he takes [the ghee] in sixteen ladlings.
Prajāpati consists of sixteen parts;
Prajāpati is Agni. Thus, he gratifies him with food that is commensurate with his own self.
For that food which is commensurate with one's own self protects it and does not injure it; whereas that which is more injures it, and that which is less does not satisfy it.
He takes [the butter] in a common *sruva*-ladle, for he whom he gratifies here is common to all. He offers with two verses addressed to Viśvakarman;

this Agni is Viśvakarman, and it is him he thus gratifies. He offers three oblations; Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food he gratifies him. 9.2.2. [3]
Then he places the fuel-sticks.

It is just as if, after satisfying [someone], one were to serve them food; so it is here. They are made of Udumbara wood; for the Udumbara is strength and sap. He thus gratifies him with that very strength and sap. They are moist; for this indeed—
That which is the unharmed, living, moist part of the trees—with that very unharmed, living, moist part of the trees he thus gratifies him. They are placed in ghee; for ghee belongs to Agni;
he thus gratifies him with his own portion, with his own essence. They remain there throughout the entire night, for it is there that they possess that essence.
They amount to three; he places three kindling-sticks (samidh). Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food he thus gratifies him.
Furthermore, as to why he offers these oblations:
For the gods, when they were about to go forth, prepared him beforehand with food by means of these oblations;
in the same way, this sacrificer now prepares him beforehand with food by means of these oblations as he is about to go forth. 9.2.2 [5]
He indeed takes up the fivefold-obtained [offering];
for this vital breath in the head is distributed fivefold— mind, speech,
breath, eye, and ear— and it is this very fivefold-distributed vital breath in the head that he thereby places within him.

With the verse, "Agni takes up [the fuel] with his sharp flame," he sharpens its head with this verse containing the word "sharp" (*tigma*), for the sake of sharpness. Then he draws sixteen ladlefuls;
there are eight vital breaths and eight limbs—this constitutes the correspondence in the same [verse].
He takes [the butter] in the *sruc* spoon, for the limbs and the vital breaths exist together within the self;
he offers separately, thereby establishing a distinction between the limbs and the vital breaths; he offers with two verses addressed to Viśvakarman.
This Agni is Viśvakarman; it is him that he thus prepares. He offers three oblations; Agni is threefold: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food does he prepare him.
With seventeen verses; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, and Prajāpati is Agni: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—so much does he prepare him.

In this way he prepares him by means of that which is taken up twenty-one times: there are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first; it is for the sake of this correspondence.
And furthermore, as to why he puts on these kindling-sticks.
The gods, having prepared him completely and in his entirety, then gratified him with this food— namely, with these kindling-sticks (*samidh*); in the very same way, this sacrificer,
having prepared him completely and in his entirety, now gratifies him with this food— namely, with these *audumbara* kindling-sticks.

They become moist and, placed in clarified butter, remain there for the entire night; its etymological explanation (*bandhu*) has been stated. With the mantra, "Lead him upward, lead him further forward, O Indra; in whose house we perform the oblation," he offers three fuel-sticks; Agni is threefold—so great as Agni is, so great is his measure.
By this much food he thus gratifies him. He offers three oblations; that makes six, the significance of which has been explained.
9.2.3 [1] Now, therefore, he issues the command: "Lift up the fuel, hold out the under-layering grass, for Agni!"
"Recite for the one being struck; O Āgnīdhra, follow with the single *sphyā*-stick; O Brahman, mutter the *Apratiratha* hymn.
For when the gods were about to advance toward this sacrifice, as they were spreading it out, the Asuras and Rakṣases [assailed them] from the south.
"The destroyers wish to strike us; you will not sacrifice, nor will you extend that sacrifice," [they said].
Those gods then spoke to Indra:
"You indeed are the best among us, the strongest, and the most heroic; you [should take] these..."

"Be on guard against the *rakṣases*! "Then let the *brahman* be my second," he said. "So be it," they replied. For him, they made Bṛhaspati his second; for Bṛhaspati is indeed the *brahman*. Having driven away the Asuras, the *rakṣases*, and the destroyers from the south by means of both Indra and Bṛhaspati, they performed this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction. 9.2.3 [4]
This very thing is performed now which the gods performed; however, those *rakṣas* were already driven away by the gods.
When he performs this, it is with the thought, "I shall do what the gods did," and furthermore, it is by means of both Indra and Bṛhaspati.
Having struck away the *surās*, the *rakṣas*, and the destroyers from the south, he extends this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction.
That which is Indra is this very Apratiratha; and that which is Bṛhaspati is this very Brahman.

Now, as for the fact that the Brahman priest mutters the *Apratiratha* hymn: it is by means of Indra and Bṛhaspati that he thus drives away the Asuras, the Rakṣases, and the destructive spirits from the south; having cleared them away, he extends this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction.
Therefore, the Brahman priest mutters the *Apratiratha*. 9.2.3. [6]
"Swift, sharpening his horns, terrible like a bull"—these twelve verses addressed to Indra are appropriate; there are twelve months in a year, and the year is Agni.
As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just so much does he [establish it] here on the south side.

The *triṣṭubh* verses drive away the Asuras, the Rakṣases, and the destroyers. The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus drives away the Asuras, the Rakṣases, and the destroyers from the south. These amount to twenty-two *gāyatrī* verses; they are dedicated to Agni, for this is a rite pertaining to Agni.
Then he lifts it up with the verse:
"May all the gods lift thee up, O Agni, with their thoughts"; the significance of this has already been explained.
Then they proceed toward [the altar].
"May the divine goddesses protect the sacrifice in the five directions. Both the gods and the Asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, contended for the directions.

The gods wrested the directions from the Asuras; in the same way, the sacrificer now wrests the directions from his hateful rival. By saying "the divine," he makes them divine; [he says] "may they protect the sacrifice."

"May the goddesses protect this sacrifice"—this means "the divine ones. "Driving away lack of mind and evil thought"—lack of mind (*amati*) is indeed hunger; thus, "driving away hunger," this is what it means. "Bestowing upon the lord of the sacrifice a share in the increase of wealth"—wealth (*rayi*) and nourishment (*poṣa*), this is what it means:
"bestowing upon the lord of the sacrifice a share in both wealth and nourishment. "The sacrifice has stood upon the increase of wealth"—upon both wealth and nourishment.
"And the sacrifice has mounted upon it"—this refers to [the verse]:
"Upon the kindled fire, being magnified. The sacrificer is indeed "magnified," and "winged with hymns" refers to the *ukthas*.
"His leaves are worthy of praise"—this means "worthy of sacrifice. "Seized"—this means "held.
"Taking hold of the heated *gharma*, they sacrificed"—for indeed, taking hold of this heated *gharma*, they sacrificed.
"When the gods sacrificed the sacrifice with vigor (*ūrj*)"—for indeed, the gods sacrificed this sacrifice with vigor. 9.2.3 [10]
"To the divine supporter, the most pleasing one"—for he is indeed the divine supporter and the most pleasing;

"the one of divine glory, of auspicious mind, with a hundred paths"—for he is indeed of divine glory, of auspicious mind, and has a hundred paths; "having encompassed him, the gods went to the sacrifice."
"Having taken hold of this, the gods went to the sacrifice; the gods stood ready as *adhvaryus* for the gods"—for the sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*;
"the gods stood ready as those worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*) for the gods"—this is what it means.
"May you two enjoy the oblation; may the *śamitṛ* prepare it for the sacrifice."
"What has been offered, what has been well-offered"—this is the fourth sacrifice, wherein the oblation goes.

The Adhvaryu mutters the *yajuṣ* formulas from the front; the Hotṛ recites the *ṛc* verses from behind; the Brahman mutters the *Apratiratha* hymn from the south. This indeed is the fourth sacrifice; may the utterances and blessings favor us.
"Then may our words and blessings be accepted"—this is [the meaning].
"Sūrya, with rays and golden hair, in the east;
Savitṛ, the light, has raised his eternal beam"—this indeed is that Āditya.

"Agni is he; he is the sun-rayed, golden-haired Savitṛ who raises up this imperishable light in the east. At his impulsion, Pūṣan goes forth, the knowing one. Pūṣan, indeed, is cattle; they move forth at his impulsion. "Beholding all beings, the guardian"—for he indeed beholds all this, and he alone is the guardian of this entire world.
The protectors (goptṛ).
9.2.3.[13] Now, those five intermediate directions that are below yonder sun—those the gods wrested away from the Asuras; and so too those [others].

Thus, by ascending these very [bricks], the sacrificer appropriates those [powers] from his hateful rival; furthermore, he ascends them himself. Moreover, it was by means of these that the gods attained this goal from here, and in the same way, by means of these, this [sacrificer] now attains this goal from here. 9.2.3. [14]
Then he lays down a speckled stone.
Yonder sun, indeed, is the speckled stone;
it is yonder sun that he thus lays down. It is speckled, for the disk is speckled by means of its rays.

He places it between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya fires. The Gārhapatya is indeed this world, and the Āhavanīya is the sky; he thus places it between these two worlds. Therefore, it burns between these two worlds. 9.2.3 [15]
At the place of the Āgnīdhra.

The Āgnīdhra is indeed the intermediate space; he thus places him in the intermediate space. Therefore, he has the intermediate space as his abode; at every stage, for he is here at every stage. 9.2.3 [16]
This is that very breath; he thus places breath within himself. This is life; he thus places life within himself.
This is food, for this life is indeed food, and food is indeed life. It becomes a stone, for a stone is firm; life is indeed firm.

He makes it speckled; for food is, as it were, speckled. 9.2.3.[17] He lays it down with the words: "This measurer sits in the midst of heaven," for he is indeed the measurer who sits in the midst of heaven.

"He has filled the two worlds and the intermediate space"—for as he rises, he indeed fills these worlds; "he looks upon all the ghee-dripping ones"—this refers to the offering-spoons and the altars; "between the former and the latter sign"—this means between this world and that world;
and furthermore, it refers to both that which is being piled here now and that which was piled there previously. 9.2.3 [18]

"The bull, the ocean, the ruddy one, the fair-winged"—for he is indeed the bull, the ocean, the ruddy one, the fair-winged. "He has entered the womb of the ancient father"—for he enters this womb of the ancient father; "placed in the midst of heaven."

"Pṛśni, the stone"—for he is indeed placed in the middle of the sky; "the speckled-stoned one has strode out; he guards the two ends of the mid-region"—for as he strides out, he goes to the ends of these worlds.
With two verses he lays it down.
The sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much he thus lays him down.
He does so with two Triṣṭubh verses, for he (Agni) is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh. He does not settle it, for he is unsettled;
nor does he pronounce the *sūdadohas* verse over it, for the *sūdadohas* is breath, and this (Agni) is breath—what [breath] would be in breath?
Thinking, "I shall preserve it," he deposits it so that it may not perish.
Then they approach with the verse, "Indra have all strengthened," the significance of which has been explained; and [they recite], "The sacrifice is the invocation of the gods."
"May the sacrifice bring us well-being; may it bring [us] hither," for the sacrifice indeed calls upon the gods and calls upon for well-being;
"may the god Agni sacrifice to the gods and bring them hither," that is to say, "may the god Agni both sacrifice and carry [the offerings] to the gods. 9.2.3. [21] "The impulse of strength..."
"With the lifting-up, Indra has lifted up my rivals; with the pressing-down, he has pressed them down beneath me.
As the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*). 9.2.3.[22] Both the lifting-up and the pressing-down.
"Brahman and the gods have strengthened me; now, O Indra and Agni, scatter my rivals in all directions. As the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance.
Now, as for those four quarters that are above yonder sun—
The gods then wrested these from the Asuras; moreover, they ascended them.
In the same way, the sacrificer now wrests them from his hateful rival and likewise ascends them. Furthermore, it was by means of these that the gods [attained] this.

Just as they attained [the world of heaven], so does this one attain it from here. 9.2.3.[24] Then they ascend the fire with the verse, "Step forth with Agni toward the vault," for the vault is indeed the heavenly world.

"Go forth by this fire to this heavenly world," he says; "bearing the *ukhya* in your hands," for they indeed bear the *ukhya* fire in their hands; "having gone to the back of heaven, the heavenly world, dwell in harmony with the gods," that is to say, "having gone to the back of heaven, the heavenly world, dwell in harmony with the gods. 9.2.3 [25]

"Go forth, O wise one, along the eastern direction"—the eastern direction indeed belongs to Agni; thus it means, "Go forth, O wise one, along your own direction. "O Agni, may there be an Agni before you"—[it means] "you, O Agni, [be] the Agni before this Agni."

"Be thou Agni"—this means "shine forth, illuminating all quarters. "Shine forth, illuminating all quarters"—this means "shine forth, illumining every direction. "Bestow strength upon our bipeds and quadrupeds"—with these words he invokes a blessing. 9.2.3.[26] "From the earth, I..."

"I have ascended the intermediate space; from the intermediate space I have ascended to heaven"—for they go from the *gārhapatya* fire to the *āgnīdhrīya*, and from the *āgnīdhrīya* to the *āhavanīya*.
"From the back of the firmament of heaven, I have gone to the light of heaven"—this means, "From the back of the firmament of heaven, I have gone to the world of heaven. 9.2.3 [27]
"Those going to heaven do not look back;

they ascend to the sky, to both worlds"—for indeed those who go to the heavenly world do not look back, they who, being well-knowing, have spread the sacrifice that flows in every direction; this indeed is the sacrifice.
"Flowing in every direction"—these indeed are the truly wise who extend this [sacrificial thread].
"O Agni, go forward as the first among those seeking the gods"—he says this of this very Agni: "Go forward as the first among these."
"May they seek the gods"—this is the eye of both gods and mortals; "of both these, gods and men," he means.
"Desiring to sacrifice, in harmony with the Bhr̥gus"—that is, "the sacrificers, in harmony with the Bhr̥gus.
"May the sacrificers go to heaven in well-being"—that is, "may the sacrificers go to the heavenly world in well-being. 9.2.3 [29]
Those five directions which are in yonder world, those the gods wrested from the Asuras; and then they ascended them.
In the same way, the sacrificer wrests them from his hateful rival and then ascends them.
In this way he ascends it; moreover, by means of these [verses], the gods then attained this very state, and in the same way, by means of these, he now attains this very state.
Then he makes an oblation over it.
The gods indeed gratified him with food from above after he had gone;

likewise, this sacrificer now gratifies him with food from above with this oblation. It is with the milk of a black cow with a white calf: the black cow with a white calf is the night, and yonder sun is her calf.
He thus gratifies him with his own portion, with his own essence; while being held above, for he whom he gratifies is indeed above. By means of milking, for by milking milk is given. 9.2.3.
[31] And as to why he offers over it:
Agni is the head of this sacrifice, and milk is the breath; thus he bestows breath upon the head.

He should offer the oblation so that it flows toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, for the *svayamātṛṇṇā* is the breath and this [milk] is the essence; he thereby connects and unites the head and the breath with the essence. [He recites: "Night and Dawn, of one mind, though diverse in form..."
Its kinship has been stated [in the preceding section]:
"O Agni, thousand-eyed.
Indeed, he is thousand-eyed by means of the gold chips; and as for the phrase "hundred-headed," it refers to that which is yonder.

"Rudra with a hundred heads was created; a hundred are your out-breaths (*prāṇa*), a thousand your diffused breaths (*vyāna*). Indeed, he who has a hundred heads has a hundred out-breaths and a thousand diffused breaths. "Of a thousandfold wealth you are the lord"—this means "you are the lord of all prosperity.
"To that [wealth] of yours, we pay homage for the sake of vigor (*vāja*); *svāhā*!"—this, indeed, is vigor; he thus gratifies him. 9.2.3. [33]
He offers with two [verses]. The sacrificer has two feet; the sacrificer is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just that much he thus offers for him. 9.2.3 [34]

Then he places it down with the words, "Thou art a well-winged Garuḍa. For having fashioned him there as a well-winged Garuḍa, he now fashions him as a well-winged Garuḍa; he piles him up as a well-winged Garuḍa, as a well-winged Garuḍa.
Having prepared it, he finally places it on the back of the earth with the mantra: "Sit down; fill the mid-air with splendor;
prop up the sky with light; spread out the quarters with brilliance. For in this way, he performs all this.
"Being invoked, fair-faced in the east... [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.4.43].

"Being invoked, fair-faced, in front of us"—this refers to [the verse] "O Agni, sit properly in your womb. This indeed is his own womb; "sit properly therein" is what it means. "In this dwelling-place, in the higher one"—the sky is indeed the higher dwelling-place. "May all the gods and the sacrificer sit down" [is the meaning].

He settles that [offering] with the Viśve Devas together for the sacrificer; he deposits it with two verses—the significance of this has been explained—and with the *vaṣaṭ* call, the significance of which is likewise explained above. 9.2.3.
[36] Then he places fuel-sticks upon it.
The gods, indeed, gratified him with food from above—both with kindling-sticks and with oblations—when he had gone there;
in the same way, this [sacrificer] now gratifies him with food from above, both with kindling-sticks and with oblations. 9.2.3. [37]
He indeed places the first kindling-stick of *śamī* wood.
For when this oblation had been offered, he (Agni) blazed up and flared forth; therefore the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest he should harm us. They [prepared] this...
They saw the *śamī* tree; with it they appeased him. Because they appeased him with the *śamī*, therefore it is called *śamī*.
In the same way, he now appeases him with the *śamī* for the sake of pacification, not for consumption. "Of Savitṛ, the most excellent... 9.2.3 [38]. That [tree] of Savitṛ, the most excellent...
"I choose the variegated, benevolent thought, beneficial to all people, which Kaṇva milked from him—the swelling, thousand-streamed, great cow of milk. Thus Kaṇva saw her;
she, the thousand-streamed one, milked for him all desires. In the same way, for the sacrificer, she is the thousand-streamed one.
"It milks all desires.
Then he places a fuel-stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood;
its significance has already been explained: "May we worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni... (RV 8.44.16).

"Or heaven is his highest birth; let us worship with hymns in the lower dwelling-place"—the lower dwelling-place is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). "From whatever womb you have arisen, I sacrifice to that"—this is indeed his own womb; "I sacrifice to that," he means.
"To you, when kindled, they have offered oblations"—when indeed this [fire] is kindled.
At this point they offer the oblations.
Then he places a branch of *udumbara* wood;
the *udumbara* is indeed strength and sap; verily, by means of strength and sap, he gratifies him.
It has *karṇaka* fruits; for *karṇakas* are indeed cattle. Thus he gratifies him with this food, with cattle.

If he should not find one with *karṇakas*, he should offer a drop of curds and place it there. In that he offers a drop of curds, that is the form of cattle. With the verse, "O Agni, shine forth, kindled before us," he should offer a *virāj* verse; for food is a *virāj*.

By means of the Virāj, he thus gratifies him with food; he places three kindling-sticks on the fire, for Agni is threefold: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by so much food he thus gratifies him.
Then he offers oblations.

Just as one would serve and bring food, so with the *sruva* ladle he offers first and with the *sruc* ladle afterwards: "O Agni, may we today accomplish for you this hymn, like a horse, like an auspicious sacrifice that touches the heart, through our offerings"—that is, "May I accomplish for you that hymn which touches your heart. He offers with a *paṅkti* verse; the *paṅkti* has five feet, and the altar consists of five layers.
Agni is the five seasons, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just so much food does he thus gratify him.
Then he offers the oblation to Viśvakarman.
This Agni is Viśvakarman; he thus gratifies him [with the words]:

"I offer thought with mind and ghee"—that is, "I offer their thought with both mind and ghee. "So that the gods may come hither"—that is, "so that the gods may come here. "The Hotrās who increase the Truth"—that is, "who increase the Truth" (satya). For the sake of the Lord.

"Of the whole world, of the vast expanse, I offer to Viśvakarman"—that is, "I offer to him who is the lord of all this that exists, to Viśvakarman. "Every day, the oblation for the days"—that is, "the oblation is never exhausted. 9.2.3 [43] Then he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); this whole [oblation] is full; by means of the whole, he thus gratifies him. 9.2.3 [44]

"Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni"—the kindling-sticks are indeed the vital breaths, for it is the vital breaths that kindle him. "Seven tongues"—this refers to those seven persons whom they made into one person; he speaks of them here. "Seven seers"—for there were indeed seven seers. "Seven beloved abodes"—he thereby refers to the meters, for his meters are seven.

"Thou art the abodes, the dear ones; the seven priests worship thee in seven ways"—for indeed these seven priests worship him in seven ways. "Seven wombs"—this refers to the layers (of the altar). "Fill [them]," that is to say, "procreate. "With ghee"—ghee is indeed seed; thus he places seed in these worlds. "Svāhā!"—the utterance *svāhā* is the sacrifice; thus this which is here becomes fit for sacrifice.
He performs everything at once.
"Seven, seven"—the fire consists of seven layers; there are seven seasons; the year is the [fire-altar], and the year is...

As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus gratifies him. He offers three oblations; Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much food he thus gratifies him. He places three kindling-sticks upon the fire; that makes six; the significance of that has been explained. 9.2.3 [46]
Standing, he places the fuel-sticks;

for the fuel-sticks are indeed bones, and bones are, as it were, standing. Sitting, he offers the oblations; for the oblations are indeed flesh, and flesh is, as it were, sitting. The fuel-sticks are placed in between.
The outer oblations are indeed the inner bones, and the outer [oblations] are the flesh.
9.2.3.[47] Now, therefore, follows the correspondence: he offers six oblations before and six after; with six they go to the dappled stone.

With two verses he lays down the speckled stone; with four they go toward the fire; with five they ascend the fire-altar. Thus there are twenty-nine [verses], and the oblation itself is the thirtieth. With two verses he deposits the fire; that makes thirty-two.
The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables; this is that *anuṣṭubh*.
Now, those three *anuṣṭubh* verses which they complete at the Gārhapatya fire—of these, they bring this one here.
As for why they bring this one here: it is because here this entire Agni has been consecrated; he is that very one here for him.
The food he desired was not sufficient.
He said to Agni, "I shall eat the food through you. [Agni replied], "So be it. Therefore, whenever they bring this [food] here, then this [Agni]—
"He becomes sufficient for food and sufficient for oblations.
Furthermore, they say: "Prajāpati himself placed this dear son upon his breast. He who knows this thus indeed places his dear son upon his breast.
Regarding this, they say here:

"Those seven persons whom they made into one person—he is indeed this very fire that is being built; and that which was their upward prosperity and essence which they gathered together, that is this [fire]."

As for this fire which they bring here—when they bring it here, they carry upward that very prosperity and essence which belongs to these seven persons; this is his head, and this fire is his body. Having thus prepared his body, he restores the head to it. 9.3.1. [1]
Now, therefore, he offers the Vaiśvānara oblation.

At this point, this entire Agni has been consecrated; he is here the deity Vaiśvānara, and it is for him that he offers this oblation. By means of the oblation, he makes him the deity—for indeed, for whichever deity [an oblation is offered], that deity one thereby makes.
The oblation is taken for that deity for whom it is not taken; [the cake is] on twelve potsherds; twelve months are a year;
Vaiśvānara is indeed the year. 9.3.1.
[2] And as to why he offers this Vaiśvānara oblation.

He is about to generate this Agni Vaiśvānara; he pours him out there beforehand, at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, as seed. For whatever kind of seed is poured into the womb, such is what is born. Since he pours out Vaiśvānara there as seed, therefore he is here [on earth] as Vaiśvānara.

There it is performed in a whisper; for there it is seed, and seed is indeed poured out in a whisper. Here it is spoken aloud, for seed, once born, becomes manifest. 9.3.1 [3] Now, as for that Vaiśvānara...
These worlds are he; this very earth is the All, Agni is the Hero;
the atmosphere is the All, Vāyu is the Hero; the sky is the All, Āditya is the Hero.
9.3.1.[4] These worlds which are yours—these are they.

This head is that [Agni]; this very earth is his plants; the beard is that [earth]. This entire universe is speech, and Agni is speech. He (Agni) is above it, for Agni is indeed above this [earth]. 9.3.1. [5] This very atmosphere is [his body].

Therefore, this is hairless; for the intermediate space is, as it were, hairless. This entire universe is indeed breath (*prāṇa*), which is wind (*vāyu*); that is the man. He is in the middle of this [universe], for wind is in the middle of the intermediate space. 9.3.1. [6] The sky is indeed the head.

The stars are his hair; this entire universe is his eye, which is the sun. That man is below it, for the sun is below the sky; thus he becomes its head. Vaiśvānara is his head, and this built-up fire-altar is his body. Having prepared the body of this [altar], he thereby restores its head. 9.3.1. [7]
Then he offers to the Maruts.
The Maruts are indeed the vital breaths; thus he bestows the vital breaths upon this [sacrificer] after having offered to Vaiśvānara.

Vaiśvānara is indeed the head; he thereby places the vital breaths in the head. 9.3.1.[8] This one becomes a single [brick]; for the head is, as it were, one. The other seven are of seven potsherds; for even though [the head] is made many times over, [it remains one].

Seven by seven, indeed seven; he thereby places seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the head. This one is manifest; for the head is, as it were, manifest, while the others are unmanifest, for they are, as it were, unmanifest.
Standing, he offers this [oblation], for the head stands as it were; sitting, he offers the others, for the vital breaths sit as it were.
Now, those two first Māruta [oblations] are these two vital breaths; they are in the middle of the Vaiśvānara.
He offers [the oblations] in the middle, for these two breaths of the head are in the middle. 9.3.1.
[11] Now, as for those two second [oblations]: he offers them closer together, for these two [breaths] are, as it were, closer together.
The two vital breaths (prāṇau) [are the first two]. Now, as for those which are the third:
these two [fires] he offers more closely together, for these two are, as it were, closer together.
The vital breaths are indeed the *araṇyānucya* hymns; thus he becomes one who recites the *araṇyānucya* hymns in the forest, for with speech one encounters much that is terrible.
Furthermore, as to why he offers oblations to Vaiśvānara and the Maruts:
Vaiśvānara is the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the Maruts are the common people (*viś*); [it serves to establish] both the nobility and the common people.
He indeed makes that [oblation] for the people (*viś*); he offers the Vaiśvānara first; having thus established the ruling power (*kṣatra*), he creates the people.
This one [oblation] becomes single;
he thereby places the ruling power in a single place and places prosperity in a single place, while the others are many among the people.
He bestows its abundance.

This [sacrificial cake] is explicitly defined (*nirukta*), for the ruling power (*kṣatra*) is, as it were, explicitly defined; the others are undefined (*anirukta*), for the common people (*viś*) are, as it were, undefined.
Standing, he offers this oblation; for the ruling power (*kṣatra*) is, as it were, standing, while the other [oblations] he offers sitting; for the common people (*viś*) are, as it were, sitting.
Indeed, he offers that very one with the *puro'nuvākyā* and the *yājyā*, with the ladle at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*;

but the others he offers with his hand while sitting, with the utterance of *svāhā*. Thus, he makes the common people follow the ruling power, acting in accordance with its will and following its path.
He performs [the rite].

Regarding this, they say: "How is it that these [oblations] of his come to be offered with the *puro'nuvākyā* verses, with the *yājyā* verses, and with the *vaṣaṭ*-call by means of the *sruk* ladle? Those which are the first three feet of these seven-footed *māruta* verses constitute [the *puro'nuvākyā*].

The *gāyatrī* with three feet is the *puro'nuvākyā*; then those which are the last four [syllables] constitute the four-footed *triṣṭubh*, which is the *yājyā*. This very tuft of hair is the *kapucala*, and this staff is the *svāhākāra* or *vaṣaṭkāra*. Thus, these [oblations] of his come to possess *puro'nuvākyās* and *yājyās*, and are offered with the ladle upon the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*. 9.3.1. [18]
Now, as for why he first offers the oblation to the Maruts on the south:
those seven rivers that flow eastward, it is they that constitute this [cake] on seven potsherds;
for there are indeed seven of those which flow eastward. 9.3.1.[19]
Now, that which he offers first on the north side is the Seasons; it consists of seven potsherds, for there are seven seasons. Then, that which he offers second on the south side—

It consists of seven potsherds, for there are seven domestic animals; he offers it immediately after the previous one, thereby establishing the animals in the waters. 9.3.1.[21] Now, as for that second [oblation] which he offers on the northern [fire]:

There are seven seers; that [cake] consists of seven potsherds, for there are indeed seven seers. He offers it immediately after the previous one; thus he establishes the seers within the seasons. Now, as for that which he offers thirdly on the south side—
The vital breaths are seven; that cake consists of seven potsherds, for there are indeed seven vital breaths in the head.
He offers it immediately after the previous one; thus he places the vital breaths in the head without interruption.
Now, as for the third one which he offers on the north side—

It consists of seven potsherds, for there are seven meters, each increasing by four syllables; he offers it immediately after the previous one, and thus he places the meters immediately after the Ṛṣis. 9.3.1 [24]
Now, as for those seven rivers that flow westward—that is the one to be recited in the forest;
it consists of seven potsherds, for there are indeed those seven which flow westward. That is this downward vital breath of this Prajāpati; thus it is the one to be recited in the forest.
The forest is, as it were, hidden; the downward breath is, as it were, hidden. Therefore, those who drink from these rivers become more deceitful, more slanderous, and more prone to harsh speech.
When he says, "This is for the Maruts," he makes this food for him and presents it to him; thereby he gratifies him. 9.3.1 [25]
That Vaiśvānara is indeed yonder sun; and those Maruts are its rays. Those [cakes] on seven potsherds each become sevenfold, for the hosts of the Maruts are sevenfold. 9.3.1. [26]
He offers oblations with the formulas: "Śukrajyotis, Citrajyotis, Satyajyotis, and Jyotiṣmān"—these are their names.
Having thus prepared this disk (the sun), he then assigns these rays to it by mentioning their names.
9.3.2. [1] Now, therefore, he offers the Vasordhārā.
Herein this entire fire has been consecrated; he is here as Vasu, and for him the gods drew forth this stream and gratified him with it.
Because the Vasus drew forth this stream for him, therefore they call it the "Stream of Wealth" (vasordhārā); in the same way, this [sacrificer] now draws forth this stream for him.
He takes hold of him with it; thereby he gratifies him.
And as to why he offers this stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*):
this is indeed his consecration (*abhiṣeka*); for by this, the gods [bestowed] everything upon him.
Having thus completely consecrated him, they then anointed him with these objects of desire by means of this *vasordhārā*.

In the same way, this [sacrificer] now, having completely consecrated him, anoints him with these objects of desire by means of this *vasordhārā*—with clarified butter taken five times, using a ladle of *udumbara* wood; the significance of that has already been explained. 9.3.2. [3]
Having offered to Vaiśvānara— the head, indeed, is Vaiśvānara, and it is through the head that food is eaten; moreover,
it is from the head that one being consecrated is consecrated— having offered to the Maruts— the vital breaths, indeed, are the Maruts, and it is by means of the vital breaths that food is eaten.
Now, he is consecrated in the vital breaths when he is being consecrated.
That [consecration] indeed takes place in the *araṇyānūkya*.
The *araṇyānūkya* is speech; food is eaten by means of speech, and furthermore, it is by means of speech that [the consecration occurs].

While being consecrated, he is consecrated; all this is wealth (*vasu*), for all these are desires. This stream consists of wealth (*vasumayī dhārā*), just as [the flow] of milk or clarified butter; even so, having begun with this very [intention], this oblation of clarified butter is offered.
Because this is a stream consisting of wealth, therefore they call it "The Bestower of Wealth" (*vasodhārā*). 9.3.2. [5]

He says: "This for me and this for me; with this I gratify you and with this, and with this I consecrate you and with this"—and furthermore, "Give this to me and give this to me. As soon as this stream reaches the fire, then he should proceed with this *yajus* formula. 9.3.2. [6]
The gods, having gratified him with this food, having consecrated him with these desires, and having sprinkled him with this stream of wealth (vasordhārā),
