then requested these desires from him; and he, being sacrificed for, gratified, and consecrated, granted them to them.

He bestowed these desires upon him; in the very same way, he now bestows them upon this [sacrificer]. Having gratified him with this food, having consecrated him with these desires, and having sprinkled him with this stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*), he then begs these desires for him. To him—being sacrificed for, gratified, and consecrated—he bestows these desires. He joins the desires in pairs so that there may be no separation, as in the case of two people living together in one house.
"One should unite [the sacrifice] with the formula: 'May they be made ready by the sacrifice.
(9.3.2.7) Indeed, the gods said: "By what means shall we receive these desires? They replied: "By the self alone; [it is] the sacrifice."

The sacrifice is indeed the self of the gods, and it is likewise the self of the sacrificer. When he says, "May they prosper through the sacrifice," he thereby says, "May they prosper through my very self. He causes them to prosper during twelve [months].

Twelve months are a year, and the year is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food he thus gratifies him, and with just so much food he thus consecrates him. He prepares it on fourteen potsherds, he prepares it on eight potsherds, [and] on ten potsherds.
He ordains it among the thirteen; he ordains it in nine.
9.3.2.[9] Then he offers the *ardhendrāṇi* oblations.
All this is the *ardhendrāṇi*; by means of all this, he thus gratifies him. Moreover—
In this way, he consecrates him with everything. 9.3.2.[10] Then he offers the *graha* libations.
The *grahas* are indeed the sacrifice; thus, by means of the sacrifice as food, he gratifies him. Furthermore—
By means of this very sacrifice, he thus consecrates him with food. 9.3.3.
[1] Then he offers these sacrificial rites:
"Agni and my Gharma..."
Thus, by means of these very sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*), he gratifies him;
moreover, by means of these very sacrificial rites, he consecrates him.
Then he offers the odd-numbered *stoma*s.

Having obtained all desires through the *yuj* and *stoma* chants, the gods indeed went to the heavenly world; in the very same way, the sacrificer, having obtained all desires through the *yuj* and *stoma* chants, goes to the heavenly world.
That [series] begins with the thirty-threefold [stoma].

The thirty-three-fold [stoma] is indeed at the end of the odd-numbered stomas; it was from the very end that the gods went to the heavenly world, and in the same way, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world from the very end.
Then he offers with the even-numbered [stomas].
The meters indeed said this: "The odd-numbered *stomas* are exhausted;

let us go to the heavenly world by means of the even-numbered *stomas*. They went to the heavenly world by means of the even-numbered *stomas*; in the very same way, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world by means of the even-numbered *stomas*. 9.3.3. [5]

"Or rather, it is from the forty-eightfold [stoma]," he says. The forty-eightfold is indeed the end of the even-numbered stomas; thus the meters went to the heavenly world from the very end. In the same way, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world from the very end. 9.3.3. [6]

He says: "One for me, three for me, four for me, eight for me. Just as one climbing a tree would ascend by grasping each higher branch, so it is when he offers the *stomas*; for the *stomas* are indeed food—it is with food that he thus consecrates him. 9.3.3. [7]
Then he offers the *vayaḥ* oblations.
The *vayas* are indeed cattle; verily, by means of cattle as food, he thus gratifies him;
moreover, by means of cattle as food, he thus consecrates him. 9.3.3. [8]
Then he offers while pronouncing the names.
For the gods, having obtained all desires, then gratified him directly; in the same way, the sacrificer, having obtained all desires, then gratifies him directly.
"He gratifies him with the words, 'To strength, svāhā! To impulsion, svāhā! These are his names;
by mentioning these names, he thus gratifies him.
There are thirteen such names."
The year consists of thirteen months, and there are thirteen layers of earth for the fire-altar; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with that much he thus gratifies him.
And as to why he offers while mentioning the name:
He thus consecrates him by mentioning his name.

Then he says: "This is your kingdom; you are a restrainer for Mitra, a controller, for strength you, for rain you, for lordship over creatures you. Food indeed is strength, and food is rain; with food he thus gratifies him.

And as to why he says: "This is thy kingdom; thou art Mitra's controller, O controller, for strength thee, for rain thee, for the sovereignty of creatures thee"—this means, "This is thy kingship; thou hast been consecrated. He thus addresses him with this: "Thou art the controller of Mitra, O controller, and thou art for our strength, and thou art for our rain, and thou art for the sovereignty of our creatures. It is for this very purpose that he speaks to him.
"For all this, for all this, we have consecrated you"— therefore, indeed, they address a consecrated human king with these words.
Then he offers the ritual portions (kalpas).

The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the *kalpas*; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon this [sacrificer]. With the words, "May life prosper through the sacrifice! May the vital breath prosper through the sacrifice! he bestows those very vital breaths, made prosperous, upon him. He offers twelve *kalpa* oblations.

Twelve months make a year; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just so much he bestows these well-ordered vital breaths (*prāṇa*) upon him. And as to why he offers the *kalpa* oblations: the *kalpas* are indeed the vital breaths, and the vital breaths are immortality; it is with immortality that he thus consecrates him. 9.3.3 [14]
Then he says: "The Stoma and the Yajus, the Ṛc and the Sāman, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara. This is indeed the threefold science (trayī vidyā).
The threefold science is food; verily, by means of food he thus gratifies him. Moreover, by means of food he thus consecrates him. "To the light, O gods, we have gone;
we have become immortal," for he indeed goes to the light and becomes immortal. "We have become the offspring of Prajāpati," [he says].
For from Prajāpati comes progeny; "veṭ svāhā" is indeed the *vaṣaṭ*-call in its transcendent form, since the *veṭ*-call is the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
Food is offered to the gods either with the *vaṣaṭ*-call or with the *svāhā*-call;
thus he gratifies him with both of these, namely with the *vaṣaṭ*-call and the *svāhā*-call. Furthermore—

With these two [ladles] he thus consecrates him; at this point he throws that ladle into the fire so that whatever is smeared with ghee there shall not remain outside the fire. Now, concerning this very stream of wealth (vasordhārā):
The sky itself is its body; the clouds are its udder, lightning its teat, and the rain-stream is the stream itself.
From the sky it comes down to the earth.
Of that [cow], the cow itself is the body.
The udder itself is the udder; the teat is the teat; the stream is indeed the stream from the cow, over the sacrificer.
9.3.3.[17] Of her, the sacrificer himself is the body;
the arm is the udder, the ladle is the teat, and the stream is indeed the stream from the sacrificer.

From the gods [he obtains] the gods; from the cow, the cow; from the cow, the sacrificer. This food of the gods, which is infinite and inexhaustible, circulates. He who knows this thus—verily, for him this food becomes infinite and inexhaustible. Now, therefore, follows the calculation of the correspondence. 9.3.3. [18]

Regarding this they say: "How does this stream of wealth (vasordhārā) of his reach Agni for a year? How is it made to correspond with Agni and the year? Now, this stream of wealth consists of six hundred and three;
then there are six, and then thirty-five. Of these, as many as are the six hundred and three, so many are the days of the year.
By this, he obtains the days of the year; and those which are six, or rather the six seasons, by that he obtains the nights of the seasons.
Thus he obtains both the days and nights of the year. And as for the thirty-five [bricks], that is the thirteenth month: it is the self (*ātman*);
the thirty are the self, the two are the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), the two are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the head itself is the thirty-fifth. So great indeed is the year.
In this way, indeed, this stream of wealth (vasordhārā) of his reaches Agni for a year; thus it becomes one with Agni for a year.
For so many bricks as are possessed of sacrificial formulas (yajuṣmatya) are laid down in the middle of the Śāṇḍila fire-altar;
these bricks are indeed separate fires. In this way, these fires of his are separately offered with the stream of wealth.
They say this: "How does this stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*) of his attain the Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*), and how is it completed by means of the Great Hymn?
It is because of these very nine initial sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) of the stream of wealth that there is the *trivṛt* hymn-strophe; and then...

Those which are the forty-eight, those two twenty-four-fold fortnights, and then those which are twenty-five—this is the twenty-five-fold self; then those which are twenty-one—that is the twenty-one-fold tail; then those which are thirty-three—that is the Vaśa hymn;
and then those which are the eighty—that is the attainment of the eighties, for by means of the eighties the Mahaduktha is proclaimed. Then...

That which comes after the eighty, that which is beyond the great *uktha*—this is its [the *vasordhārā*’s] portion. Thus indeed does this *vasordhārā* attain the great *uktha*, and thus it is completed by means of the great *uktha*.
9.3.4. Now, therefore, he offers the *vājaprasavīya* oblation.
Food indeed is *vāja*; this [rite] is for the production of food for him; by means of this, he brings forth food for him. 9.3.4.
[2] This, indeed, the gods [did for him].
Having gratified him with this food, having consecrated him with these desires, and with this stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*), they then gratified him further;
in the same way, this [sacrificer] now, having gratified him with this food, having consecrated him with these desires, and with this stream of wealth, gratifies him further. 9.3.4. [3]
And as to why he offers this Vājaprasavīya oblation:

this is indeed his consecration (abhiṣeka). For the gods, having gratified him with this food and having consecrated him with these desires by means of this stream of wealth (vasordhārā), then further [honored] him thus.

In this very way they consecrated him; and so does this [sacrificer] now: having gratified him with this food, having consecrated him with these desires, and with this stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*), he then consecrates him once again. 9.3.4.
It consists of all kinds of herbs.
All this food consists of all herbs;

thus he gratifies him with all food, and moreover, he consecrates him with all food. He should set aside one of those foods and not eat it for as long as he lives, using [a vessel] made of udumbara wood.
With a cup made of Udumbara wood and with a dipping-spoon (sruva), the significance of these two has been explained. They have four corners; for there are four quarters.
He thus gratifies him with food from all the quarters; moreover, he thus consecrates him with food from all the quarters. 9.3.4. [5]
And as to why he offers this Vājaprasavīya oblation: these very deities have been pressed by this pressing for which he is about to press;
it is them he thus gratifies, and they, being sacrificed to and gratified, [bestow] this upon him.

They all give their consent; he who is consecrated with their consent is consecrated. Indeed, for whomsoever the kings grant their consent to the kingdom, he becomes a king, and not he for whom they do not. In that he offers into the fire, he thereby consecrates Agni; and in that he offers to these deities, he thereby gratifies those gods who have authority over this consecration. 9.3.4. [6]
Or rather, he also offers these *pārtha* oblations.

For the gods indeed desired this: "May we be consecrated by all consecrations right here. They were consecrated by all consecrations right here; in the same way, the sacrificer [now] [is consecrated] by all consecrations right here.
It is pressed forth (sūyate).
9.3.4.[7] Those which are the *pārtha* offerings—those belong to the *rājasūya*; and in that he offers them, it is by means of the *rājasūya*.

Now, as for those fourteen [verses] that follow: of those, the seven that come first belong to the Vājapeya; when he offers them, he is consecrated by means of the Vājapeya. Then, as for the seven that follow, they belong to Agni; when he offers them, he is consecrated by means of the Agnisava. 9.3.4. [8]

He indeed performs the preliminary offerings of the Rājasūya, and then those of the Vājapeya. For one becomes a king by sacrificing with the Rājasūya and a sovereign (samrāj) by the Vājapeya; since kingship comes first and then sovereignty, therefore, having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, he [does not perform the Rājasūya].
"One should sacrifice with the Rājasūya; it is a descent [to lower status]. Just as one who is a sovereign (*samrāj*) might become a king (*rājā*), so is that.
He offers the final oblations to Agni. For all these consecrations (*sava*) are the consecration of Agni; indeed, he has been consecrated by means of the entire Agnisava."
He becomes both a king and a sovereign; therefore, he offers the most excellent oblations into this fire.
Then he consecrates him upon a black antelope skin.
The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; it is thus into the sacrifice itself that he consecrates him.
The hairs are indeed the *chandases*; he thus consecrates him with the *chandases*. To the north is its connection; it has the fringes turned eastward, for that is the way among the gods.
Now, some indeed consecrate him to the south of the fire.

"To the south is the preparation of food; therefore, let us consecrate him from half of that food"—one should not do so. This quarter indeed belongs to the ancestors; he for whom they thus consecrate quickly goes toward that quarter. 9.3.4 [12]

Some indeed consecrate him at the Āhavanīya fire, thinking, "The Āhavanīya is indeed the heavenly world; thus we shall consecrate him in the heavenly world. One should not do so, for that [Āhavanīya] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self; by means of this [human self], they would indeed deprive him of those [divine powers].
They follow after that divine self which they thus consecrate, [thinking], "By means of this mortal self, let us attain that divine self.
One should consecrate him from the north alone.
This northern-eastern direction belongs to both gods and men;
he thus consecrates him while he is dependent upon and established in his own quarter. Indeed, one who is established in his own abode does not come to harm. 9.3.4 [14]
One should consecrate a being who is seated;

for one who has already come into being is, as it were, seated. One should consecrate one who desires to become great while he is standing; for one who desires to become great is, as it were, standing. One should consecrate one who desires prosperity on a goat-skin, and one who desires power on a black antelope skin.

For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), for both [desires], or for both [results], he spreads that [skin] to the north of the tail, with the hair upwards and the neck facing east, so as to touch the enclosing stones. 9.3.4.
[15] It is placed touching the enclosing stones.

In that the black antelope skin is touched by the enclosing stones, his divine self becomes consecrated upon the black antelope skin; and in that he sprinkles him while he stands touching the fire, he is thus not severed from this divine consecration. 9.3.4 [16]
Having offered an oblation in the fire, he then sprinkles him with that [remnant].
This is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self; for the gods were first, and then human beings.
Therefore, having offered in the fire, he sprinkles him with what remains of that very [offering]. In this regard, that [self]—
He throws the *sruva* spoon after [the oblation]. Then, having turned him around so that his right arm is toward him, he sprinkles him with the formula:
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ..."

"With the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, with the sovereign power of Agni, I consecrate him. Sarasvatī is indeed speech; all this is her restraint. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he consecrates him with all this, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, and with the sovereignty of Agni.
He consecrates him with universal sovereignty; he then throws that cup into it so that what is smeared there shall not remain outside the fire.
He indeed consecrates him in the midst of the Pārtha verses.
The *pārtha* oblations are indeed the year;

he thus places him in the middle of the year. He offers six before and six after; for there are six seasons; by means of the seasons, he thus encloses him on both sides as he is being consecrated. Bṛhaspati...

Indra is the highest of those who came before, and the first of those who come after; Bṛhaspati is indeed the *brahman*, and Indra is the *kṣatra*. With both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*, he thus encompasses on both sides the one who has been consecrated. 9.4.1. Now, therefore, he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* (kingdom-sustaining) oblations.

The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are indeed kings, for they sustain the kingdoms; these deities are consecrated by this very consecration (*sava*) by which he is about to be consecrated. He thus gratifies them;
they, being sacrificed to and gratified, grant their approval for this consecration. With their approval, he is consecrated—whomever the kings [approve].

They authorize him to rule; he becomes a king, and not he who does not [authorize him]. Since kings support kingdoms, these gods are indeed kings; therefore, these [oblations] are called *rāṣṭrabhṛt* (king-supporters).
Furthermore, as to why he offers these *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations:

From Prajāpati, as he was relaxed, pairs issued forth, having become Gandharvas and Apsarases. Having become a chariot, he went around them; having gone around them, he took them into himself and made them his own.
In the same way, this [sacrificer], having gone around them, now takes them into himself and makes them his own. 9.4.1. [3]

He who was that Prajāpati who became dismembered is this very Agni who is now being built up; and those pairs which went forth from him are these very deities to whom he now offers this oblation. 9.4.1 [4]
He offers to the Gandharvas and Apsarases;

for having become Gandharvas and Apsarases, they ascended [from this world], and moreover, it is by means of fragrance and beauty that Gandharvas and Apsarases move about; therefore, whoever approaches a woman in sexual union [is said to do so].
He desires both fragrance and form.
He offers oblations of pairs;
for from a pair, indeed, comes procreation, and he who is procreated becomes the sovereign.

He indeed becomes one who has no kingdom who does not procreate; for couples support the kingdom, and these gods are likewise couples. Therefore, these "kingdom-supporting" oblations are offered with clarified butter taken in twelve ladlings, and they become exactly twelve offerings; the significance of this is as follows. 9.4.1. [6]
He offers first to the male, and then to the females;
he thus endows the male with superior vigor. He offers to the male as if to one alone, and to the females as if to many; therefore, even for a single man, there are many wives.
They exist by means of both the *vaṣaṭ* call and the *svāhā* call. He offers to the male with the *svāhā* call, and likewise to the females.
Thus he endows the male alone with virility.
"The conqueror of truth, the upholder of truth... [so it is said].
"Truthful, whose abode is truth"—this refers to Agni as the Gandharva; "his Apsarases are the plants.
For Agni, the Gandharva, departed together with his mate, the Apsarases who are the plants.
"Muda by name"—the plants are indeed *muda* (delights), for by means of the plants all this world rejoices. He [Agni] is this Brahman.
"May the ruling power protect; to it, svāhā! Vāṭ! To them, svāhā!"—the significance of this has already been explained. 9.4.1. [8] "The *saṃhita* (the joined)":
yonder sun, indeed, is the *saṃhita*, for he joins together day and night. "Possessing all melodies": for he indeed...

The Sun is the Gandharva of all Sāman; his Apsarases are the rays. The Sun, as the Gandharva, went forth together with his mate, the Apsarases, the rays, under the name "Āyavaḥ" (the Drawers-in), for the rays draw themselves in like those who pull themselves up.
"May he protect this our priesthood and nobility"—the significance of this has been explained. 9.4.1. [9]
"Suṣumṇa" means "one worthy of good sacrifice. "Sūryaraśmi" [means] "having rays like the sun," for the rays of the moon are indeed like those of the sun.
"Candramas the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the constellations"—Candramas is indeed the Gandharva.
"Accompanied by the constellations and the Apsarases in pairs, he went forth; [he is] named Bhekurayas.
Indeed, they are called Bhākurayas, for the constellations produce light (*bhās*). "May he protect this our priesthood and nobility"—the significance of this has already been explained.
"Swift" means "quick. "All-pervading" (viśvavyacāḥ), for he indeed makes this entire world an expanse.
"Vāta is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the waters"—Vāta is indeed the Gandharva, and he went forth together with the waters as his Apsarases, his mates.
"He whose name is Force" (ūrjaḥ)—the waters are indeed force, for from the waters force is born. May he [grant] this Brahman and Kṣatra to us.
"May he protect us"—the significance of this has already been stated.
"Bhujyu Suparṇa": Bhujyu is indeed the sacrifice; for the sacrifice nourishes (*bhunakti*) all beings. The sacrifice...
"The Gandharva, the Apsarases as his Dakṣiṇās"—the sacrifice is indeed the Gandharva;
together with the Apsarases, the Dakṣiṇās, he went forth in union. "Stāvā by name"—the Dakṣiṇās are indeed Stāvā, for by the Dakṣiṇās the sacrifice is praised;
moreover, whoever gives a Dakṣiṇā is indeed praised. He [the sacrificer] is not [left out].
"May this Brahman protect the Kṣatra"— the significance of this has already been explained. "Prajāpati Viśvakarman"—
Prajāpati is indeed Viśvakarman, for he created all this through his mind.

The Gandharva was his; the *ṛc*s and *sāman*s were the Apsarases. Mind, as the Gandharva, departed together with the Apsarases, the *ṛc*s and *sāman*s, as his mate. "The desires" (*iṣṭayaḥ*) by name are indeed the *ṛc*s and *sāman*s, for by means of the *ṛc*s and *sāman*s they pray:
"May it be thus for us! May it be so for us! [He said: "May he protect this Brahman and Kṣatra for us."
Its connection has been stated [in 9.4.1].
Now he offers on the head of the chariot.
This is indeed that very pressing; for it is this [soma] which those deities press for him.

They give their consent with those [formulas] by which, being consented to, he is consecrated; for that man becomes a king for whom kings consent to the kingdom, and not he for whom they do not. With clarified butter taken five times, those very five oblations are offered; the significance of this has been explained. 9.4.1. [14]

From the head; or rather, he is consecrated while being sprinkled from the head, for he holds him above while sprinkling him from above. With the same mantra, for he sprinkles him with what is common [to all]. With a complete circumambulation, he thus sprinkles him from every side. 9.4.1.[15]
And again, as to why he offers on the head of the chariot:
yonder sun is indeed this chariot; for having assumed that form, Prajāpati, having encompassed these pairs, deposited them within himself and made them his own.
In the very same way, having encompassed these, he now places them within himself and makes them his own; for while being held above, he is indeed above him who,

having encompassed these pairs, placed them within himself and made them his own, using the same mantra on all sides— for he is indeed the same as he who, having encompassed these pairs, placed them within himself and made them his own on every side.
For he who has encompassed these pairs and deposited them within himself has provided a refuge from all sides.
"O Lord of the world, O Prajāpati," [he says],
for he is indeed the lord of the world, the Prajāpati, above whom you are.

"Whose home it may be," for his homes are both above and here; "for this priesthood and for this nobility," for this fire is indeed both the priesthood and the nobility; "grant great protection, svāhā!"—that is to say, "grant great shelter, svāhā! 9.4.2. Then he offers the Vāta oblations.
These worlds are indeed this fire; the wind is the *vātahomas*. He thus places the wind in these worlds;
therefore, this wind exists in these worlds.
He brings [the fuel] from outside the fire.
Or rather, that Vāyu who is in these worlds is his trusted friend; and that Vāyu who is beyond these worlds—him he places within this [altar]. 9.4.2.
Outside the altar: this altar is indeed this [earth].
Or rather, that wind which is within this [earth] is his trusted friend; and that wind which is beyond this [earth], he places that into it.
(9.4.2.4) With joined palms; for there is no such thing as an actual seizing of this [fire]. He offers with the *svāhā*-utterance, for that [wind] is indeed below the pole.
"This chariot is the Āditya; thus he places the Vāyu before the Āditya, and therefore this [wind] blows from here toward us.
"Thou art the ocean, full of mist," [he says].
"That world is indeed the ocean, Nabhasvān Ārdradānu.
For he (Vāyu) gives moisture; thus he places that Vāyu who is in yonder world into this one.
"Śambhū mayobhū abhi mā vāhi svāhā!"—that is to say, "O auspicious and pleasant one, blow toward me! 9.4.2. [6]
"You are Māruta, the host of the Maruts.
The world of the intermediate space is indeed the Māruta, the host of the Maruts;
he thus places therein that wind which is in the world of the intermediate space [with the words]: "Be auspicious, be refreshing; blow toward me, svāhā!"

"May Śiva be propitious; may he carry me hither"—this is [the meaning]. "Thou art the seeker of aid, the worshipper"—this world is indeed the seeker of aid, the worshipper; therefore, [he refers to] him who is in this world.
The wind places this [breath] within him with the words, "O you who are auspicious and refreshing, blow upon me, svāhā!"—that is to say, "O you who are propitious and pleasant, blow upon me.
He offers with three [verses]. 9.4.2.[8]
These worlds are three, and Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he places Vāyu within these worlds.
And furthermore, as to why he offers the Vāta-homas (wind-oblations).

He thus yokes this very chariot; for the gods yoked this chariot for the sake of all desires, thinking, "With it yoked, may we attain [them]," and with it yoked they attained all desires. In the same way, the sacrificer now yokes this chariot for the sake of all desires.
"He yokes with the yoked so that he may attain [all things]"—by means of that yoking, he attains all desires.
He yokes with the *vātahomas* (wind-offerings).
The *vātahomas* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); it is by means of the vital breaths that he thus yokes him. He yokes with three.

There are indeed three vital breaths: the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the up-breath (*udāna*), and the diffused breath (*vyāna*). By means of these he now yokes him. Below, below the pole; for they yoke the draft-animal below, below the pole. With both hands; for with both hands they yoke the draft-animal. Moving around and around; for they yoke the draft-animal moving around and around. 9.4.2. [11]
He first yokes the right yoke-horse, then the left yoke-horse, and then the right side-horse;
thus it is among the gods, for otherwise it is among men. He should not yoke that [horse] again, lest he should yoke what has already been yoked; however, this applies to the draft-animal.
"One should give it while saying, 'Let him eat with what is joined [to the sacrifice]'"; they carry it upward from the Adhvaryu's dwelling, for he is above;
he gives it to the Adhvaryu, for he performs his work with it; however, he should assign it at the time of the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). 9.4.2.
Then he offers the *ruṅnatī* oblations.

Here this entire fire has been consecrated; it was here that it desired splendor (*ruc*), and the gods bestowed splendor upon it by means of these *ruṅnatī* verses. In the same way, he now bestows this splendor upon it. Furthermore, as to why he offers the *ruṅnatī* verses: [the text continues].
The *ruk* departed from Prajāpati when he was relaxed. When the gods restored him, they bestowed radiance upon him with these *ruṅnatī* verses;
in the same way, this sacrificer now bestows it upon him. 9.4.2 [14]
"O Agni, those splendors of yours which are in the sun;

O gods, those splendors of yours which are in the sun—bestow splendor upon us among the Brāhmaṇas. By saying "splendor, splendor," he bestows immortality upon him, for splendor is indeed immortality. He offers three oblations.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he bestows radiance upon him.
Then he offers an oblation to Varuṇa.
At this point, this entire Agni has been consecrated; he is here the deity Varuṇa. Therefore...

He offers this oblation; thereby he makes him a deity through the oblation. For that deity for whom an oblation is taken is indeed a deity, but not she for whom it is not taken. With a verse addressed to Varuṇa, he thus gratifies him with his own self, with his own deity. 9.4.2. [16]

Furthermore, as to why he offers the oblation to Varuṇa: when Prajāpati had become relaxed, his vigor departed from him; when the gods restored him, they placed that vigor in him by means of this [oblation]. In the same way, this sacrificer now places vigor in him by means of the offering to Varuṇa.

"By the *ṛc*—Varuṇa is indeed the *kṣatra*, and the *kṣatra* is indeed vigor; by means of vigor he thus bestows vigor upon him. (9.4.2.17) "I approach you, praising with a prayer"—he thus entreats him, praising with a prayer.

"In this way the sacrificer hopes with his oblations"—this is what he hopes with his oblations. "O Varuṇa, being unangry, be mindful here"—this means "O Varuṇa, without anger, be mindful here. "O thou of wide renown, do not steal away our life"—thus he utters a prayer for the preservation of his own self. 9.4.2. [18]
Then he offers the continuous oblations of the *arka* and the *aśvamedha*.
This Agni is indeed the *arka*, and yonder Āditya is the *aśvamedha*;
when they were created, they were separate from one another, and the gods [united them] with these oblations.
Just as they [the ancient seers] maintained continuity and joined together, so too does he now maintain continuity and join them together with these oblations.
"Svar na gharmah svāhā!"—the Gharma is indeed yonder sun; he thus places yonder sun into this fire.
He establishes it with the mantra, "The golden sun, svāhā! (9.4.2.20).
This fire is the sun; he thereby establishes this fire in yonder sun (9.4.2.21).
"Gold is semen, svāhā! Indeed, that sun is the semen; he thus places it there in yonder world. "Light is gold, svāhā!"
"This Agni is light; he places that [light] here again.
"Svāhā to Sūrya, the heavenly one!
Indeed, Sūrya is yonder Āditya; he thus makes yonder Āditya the highest of this entire universe.
He places [the fire]; therefore, this [fire] is the highest of all this.
9.4.2. [24] He offers these five oblations.
The fire-altar consists of five layers; there are five seasons; the year is the year.
As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he thus extends and joins these two together.
And as to why he says, "Svāhā! The Gharma is light; svāhā! The Arka is light," these are indeed the names of this very Agni;
he thus gratifies them and makes them a deity with the oblation, for she for whom the oblation is taken is a deity.
That [name] is not taken for her who is not accepted; moreover, by mentioning their names, he thus places these very fires into this fire. He offers these five oblations;
the fire-altar consists of five layers, there are five seasons, and the year is the year.
As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food does he thus gratify him.
Now, therefore, regarding the sowing of the oblations:
whatever oblation there may be that is accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa passage...
One should know this; at this time he should offer oblations. Indeed, he yokes this chariot for the sake of desires;
whatever oblation he offers here, he offers it as one that has already been attained.
9.4.2. Regarding this they say: "He should not offer, lest he should make [the sacrifice] redundant. But he should certainly offer, for these oblations are indeed for the sake of desires.
"Indeed, desires are not sacrificed; there is nothing beyond them.
Then, having returned at the time for the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, he pours out the *dhiṣṇyas*;
these *dhiṣṇyas* are indeed fires.
He thus piles these very fires; they are the common people (*viś*), and this piled fire-altar is the ruling power (*kṣatra*). He thereby establishes both the ruling power and the common people.
He piles that [central fire-altar] first, and then these [other altars]; having thus established the ruling power, he establishes the common people.
This one becomes a single [entity].
He makes that kṣatra and that prosperity abide in one place; the others, being many, cause that confusion among the people. This [altar] consists of five layers. 9.4.3. [3] It is five-layered.

The others consist of a single layer; he thus bestows the power of the Kṣatriya with its own strength. He makes the Kṣatriya more powerful than the Viś. He piles this one upwards; he thus piles the Kṣatriya upwards by means of layers.
The others he piles crosswise; he thereby makes the Viś subservient to the Kṣatriya from below. 9.4.3. [4]
He piles this [altar] with both: with the *yajusmatī* brick and with the *lokampṛṇā* brick.

By means of the *lokampṛṇā* alone, he thus places the ruling power (*kṣatra*) above these [other bricks] through its vigor; he makes the ruling power more vigorous than the common folk (*viś*), and the common folk less vigorous than the ruling power. 9.4.3.5.
In that he piles this [altar] with the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks alone, the *lokaṃpṛṇā* is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*); thus he places the nobility within the common people (*viś*).

He piles both: those of the sacrifice and those of the fire-altar. First those of the sacrifice, then those of the fire-altar; the significance of this has been explained. Whichever sacrificial hearth (*dhiṣṇya*) he throws down, that very one he piles up; first the *āgnīdhrīya*.
For he gathers that [earth], and first he scatters it, sitting toward the south facing north; the significance of this has already been explained.
Upon it he lays down eight bricks;
the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and [Agni] is of the nature of the Gāyatrī.
As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so much of him he thus builds up. Of those [bricks], the speckled stone is the ninth;

for there are nine vital breaths—seven in the head and two downward ones—and it is these he places in him. That Agni which is deposited when the altar has been built is the tenth; for there are ten vital breaths, and the Āgnīdhra fire-altar is in the middle.
He places them in the middle; for in the middle, indeed, these vital breaths exist, moving hither and thither along the self.
He lays down twenty-one bricks on the Hotṛ’s altar.
There are indeed twenty-one enclosing-stones; their significance has been explained.

There are eleven for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, Indra is connected with the Triṣṭubh, and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin belongs to Indra. There are eight each for the others; their significance has been explained. 9.4.3. [8]
On the Mārjālīya mound there are six;

for the seasons, the fathers, are six. Indeed, the seasons, the fathers, placed him around on the south; he is their one on the south. He lays down this one here, and those ones there, as the people (viś).
He makes that *kṣatra* face toward it.
Then he encloses them with enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*). The enclosing-stones are indeed the waters; by means of the waters, he thus encircles them. He, indeed...

He places them all around; for those waters which flow in a dug channel are the nobility (*kṣatra*), while these other waters which are here as natural pools are the common people (*viś*). When he encloses that [fire-altar] with a dug channel, he thereby bestows nobility upon the nobility; he encloses the nobility with the nobility. And when he places these [bricks] all around, he thereby bestows the common people upon the common people; he encloses the common people with the common people.

He encloses them; for as many enclosing stones as there are *yajus*-bearing bricks in those [altars], so many are there in this one—for as many *yajus*-bearing bricks as belong to that [sacrifice], so many are the enclosing stones—and thus he makes the people obedient and followers, acting in accordance with the will of the ruling power.
Then he pours soil upon these;

its significance has been explained. It is done silently, for the people (viś) are undefined. Then, following the cake-offering of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, he offers the Aveṣṭi oblations to the quarters; for this [altar] is the quarters.

He offers these oblations to those [deities]; thus he makes them deities by means of the oblation. For that deity for whom an oblation is taken is indeed a deity, but not that one for whom it is not taken. There are five [oblations], for there are five directions. 9.4.3. [11] They say: "One should offer this sacrifice consisting of ten oblations; it contains all the *stomas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, and all [the elements]."
The suns, all the quarters, and all the seasons—all this is indeed this fire. He thus makes it a deity by means of the oblation.
For that deity for whom an oblation is taken is truly a deity, but not that one for whom no oblation is taken.
There are ten [verses]; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Agni is the Virāj. There are ten quarters, and Agni is the quarters. There are ten vital breaths, and the vital breaths are Agni.

As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food he thus gratifies him. Furthermore, one should indeed offer these oblations to the Devasavā; for these deities were consecrated by this very consecration.

He gratifies those very deities by means of which he is about to be consecrated; they, being sacrificed to and gratified, grant their approval for this consecration to him. With their approval, he is consecrated. For he indeed becomes a king whom other kings approve of in his kingship, and not he whom they do not. Thus, when these deities have been consecrated by this consecration, it is because these deities [have approved].
They press [the Soma] for this pressing; therefore, these are the *devasava*s (divine pressings). 9.4.3.[13] They indeed have two names each;
for he who is pressed for a pressing has two names. Indeed, for whatever pressing one is pressed, [he receives two names].
Or else, that by which he is pressed is his second name.
There are eight [syllables];
the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure.
By this much food he thus gratifies him. Regarding this they say: "One should not offer these oblations, lest one should commit an excess. One should indeed offer them;
for these oblations are offered for the sake of desires, and there is no such thing as an excess regarding desires, whatever [desire] it may be.

The sacrificial offering (havis) is set out following the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa); thus, the essence of the sacrifice (medha) is placed in the very middle of the animal itself. He offers both: that of the Soma-sacrifice (adhvara) and that of the fire-sacrifice (agni).

First that of the Soma-sacrifice, then that of the fire-sacrifice; the significance of this has been explained. The animal-cake is offered loudly, while these [other offerings] are performed in a low voice (upāṃśu), for this is indeed an iṣṭi. "Recite the invitatory prayer! Give the command! (anubrūhi preṣya).

"Recite for the Paśupuroḍāśa; recite the offering prayer"—for these [offerings] have a common Sviṣṭakṛt and a common Iḍā; the deities of the sacrifice become [unified], while the Sviṣṭakṛt remains uncombined. 9.4.3.
Then he touches him with the preceding consecration formula.

"May Savitṛ impel you for the impelments. "This King Soma here is the king of yours; he is the king of us Brāhmaṇas. Thus he sets aside the Brāhmaṇas alone and makes them unfit to be eaten. Then, in the morning, when about to commence the Prātaranuvāka...

He yokes the fire with the words, "With what is yoked may we attain all. By means of that which is yoked, he attains all desires. He yokes it at the beginning of the entire rite; thus, whatever is performed hereafter, all of that is accomplished when [the fire] is yoked. 9.4.4. [2]
He yokes [the fires] to the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*).
These enclosing-sticks are indeed fires; thus, by means of the fires, he yokes the fire. Having touched the middle enclosing-stick...
He mutters this Yajus: "I yoke Agni with power and with ghee.

Power indeed is strength; thus he means, "I yoke Agni with both strength and ghee. "The divine eagle, great in vigor"—for he is indeed the divine eagle, great in vigor by means of his smoke; "by that may we go."
"Ascending to the station of the sun, to the heavenly world, to the highest firmament"—this is what is meant.
Then, on the right side:
"These two wings of yours, O Agni, are unwithered and feathered, with which you strike away the Rakṣasas."
"By those two, may we fall into the world of the well-doers, where the first-born, ancient seers have gone"—with these words he refers to those seers. 9.4.4.
[5] Now, the subsequent ones: "Indu, Dakṣa, Śyena, Ṛtāvā, Hiraṇyapakṣa, Śakuna, Bhuraṇyu"—these are indeed the immortals.

"Gold-winged bird, immortal, thou art the sustainer; great one, seated firmly in the assembly, homage be to thee; do not harm me"—with these words he pronounces a self-consecration. Now, as for that middle *yajus*:
That is the self, and those two on either side are the wings; therefore they have wings, for they are indeed the wings.
He yokes with three [verses].
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thus yokes him.
Then, having pressed the King (Soma), he offers it in the fire.
This indeed is that pressing; this very thing is pressed for him.

The deities authorize him for consecration; authorized by them, he is consecrated. Indeed, that man whom kings authorize to rule becomes a king, and not he whom they do not authorize. Thus, when he offers an oblation into the fire, he thereby consecrates Agni. This is his divine self, which becomes consecrated with Soma, consecrated with immortality. And then...
He then consumes it; he consecrates his own self. Thus this self of his becomes consecrated with Soma, consecrated with the immortal.
Having offered it into the fire, he then consumes it.
This [fire] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self; for the gods were first, and then humans.
Therefore, having offered into the fire, he then consumes [the remainder].
Then he releases him.

Having attained that desire for which he yokes it—he being about to commence the *yajñāyajñiya* chant—[he does so]; for the *yajñāyajñiya* is indeed the heavenly world. It is for the sake of reaching this [world] that he yokes it;
thus, having attained that desire for which he yokes it, [he attains it]. 9.4.4. [11]
He indeed unyokes it before the stotra.

For if he were to unyoke it after the stotra, he would turn his back on that world of heaven and perish; but since he unyokes it before the stotra, he remains in direct contact with the world of heaven.
Having reached the world, he releases it.
He releases it at the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), for he yokes it at the enclosing-sticks; indeed, wherever they yoke a draft-animal, that very place is where one releases it.

They release that [fire]. Having touched water at the two junctions (saṃdhyā), he mutters these two *yajus* formulas; thus the two *yajus* formulas correspond to the three enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*).

"You are the head of heaven, the navel of the earth," [he says] over the southern one; "You stand supported upon the head of the universe," [he says] over the northern one—[these are] verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhan*), for this [altar] is indeed its head.
[They are recited] with two verses containing the word "water" (*apsumat*), for the *yajñāyajñīya* is the praise-hymn (*stotra*) of Agni Vaiśvānara, and it is indeed peace.
"Therefore, with two verses containing the word *ap* (water), he unyokes [the horse].
The sacrificer is two-footed; the sacrificer is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure—
By that much he releases him; he yokes him with three [verses], thus making five. The fire-altar consists of five layers (*pañca-citika*);
there are five seasons, and the year is the fire-altar. As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—so great does this become.
Now, some indeed yoke it at the *prāyaṇīya* Atirātra and release it at the *udayanīya*, for that is the form of a completed rite.
As for this liberation: one should not think, "Let us perform the form of completion for the sake of completion.
For day after day this sacrifice is extended, and day after day it is completed. Day after day he yokes it for the journey to the heavenly world;
day after day he goes to the heavenly world by means of it. Therefore, [it should be performed] day after day.
One should yoke [the mind] day after day and release it;
furthermore, just as at the *prāyaṇīya* *atirātra*, having recited the *sāmidhenī* verses, one should say: "From here on, it is the *udayanīya*."

"I shall be one who recites it again"—thinking thus, he should therefore yoke [the mind] day after day and release it day after day. Regarding this, Cāṇḍilya, having instructed the Kaṅkatīyas in the daily ritual, went forth, saying: "Day after day, for you..."
"Yoking day by day, he releases day by day"; therefore, one should indeed yoke day by day and release day by day.
Now, therefore, regarding the vow of milk:
the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*) should subsist on milk. Verily, the nectar departed from the gods.

They said, "Let us seek this through toil and austerity. So they sought it through toil and austerity. Having consecrated themselves (*dīkṣitvā*), they became observers of the milk-vow (*payovrata*). For this indeed is austerity: that one who, having consecrated himself, remains an observer of the milk-vow. They heard its sound. 9.5.1. [3] They said, "It is indeed becoming nearer; let us apply ourselves to even more austerity. So they...
They approached three nipples, but they saw them beyond that.
They said, "It is indeed closer; let us perform even more austerity. They approached two nipples, but they saw them even closer than that. 9.5.1.[5]

They said, "It has indeed become closer; let us perform even more austerity. They approached one breast; they mastered it, but they were not able to grasp it. 9.5.1 [6] They said, "We have indeed mastered it, but we are not able to grasp it; let us perform all our austerity. On the day of preparation (upavasatha), they...
"They would have met with destruction; for this fasting is indeed all austerity. Therefore, one should not eat on the day of preparation.
9.5.1. [7] Having approached that in the morning and having pressed the Soma, they offered it into the fire; thus they placed immortality into the fire for all.

This Agni is the self (ātman) of the gods; therefore, when they placed immortality in Agni, they placed immortality in their own selves, and from that the gods became immortal. That which is this immortality is Soma.
Even today, the sacrificer seeks it through toil and austerity; having been initiated, he becomes one whose vow is milk.
This indeed is austerity: that one who, having been initiated, remains as one whose vow is milk—he hears its sound, saying, "The purchase is on such-and-such a day. 9.5.1. [9]
He approaches three teats;
he sees them from afar. He approaches two teats; he sees them more closely.
He approaches one teat; he reaches it, yet he is not able to seize it—at the time of the Upavasatha.
"This fasting leads to non-destruction; indeed, all austerity is fasting. Therefore, one should not eat on the day of preparation (upavasatha).
Having approached that [fire] in the morning and having pressed [the Soma], he offers it into the fire; thus he places immortality in the fire, and then he consumes it.
Then he places that nectar within himself; he becomes immortal. This indeed is the immortality of a human being:
that he reaches the full span of life. And so, by means of this self, he reaches the full span of life. Having offered it into the fire, he then consumes it.
This [fire] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self; for the gods were first, and then humans.
Therefore, having offered into the fire, he then consumes [the remains].
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings.

Both the gods and the asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, came to their father Prajāpati’s inheritance: namely, speech, both truth and falsehood; for they both spoke the truth and both spoke the falsehood. Speaking alike, they were indeed alike. 9.5.1 [13]
Those gods, having abandoned falsehood, took hold of truth; the Asuras, indeed, having abandoned truth, took hold of falsehood. Then this Truth looked upon this world.
When the gods had cast off falsehood among the Asuras and seized upon truth, [the latter thought], "Come, let me go after that"; so it went toward the gods. Then falsehood looked back at them. 9.5.1.
[15] Falsehood indeed looked upon them.
When the gods or the asuras, having abandoned truth, took hold of untruth, thinking, "Come, let us take that [truth]," it went over to the asuras.

They were as if more heroic and as if less wealthy; therefore, indeed, he who speaks the truth with attachment becomes as if more heroic and as if less wealthy, yet in the end he truly prospers, for it was the gods who in the end prospered. 9.5.1 [17]
Then the Asuras, speaking untruth out of attachment, became like saline soil; they were as if impoverished.
Therefore, indeed, he who speaks untruth out of attachment becomes like saline soil; he becomes as if impoverished. But in the end, he surely perishes.
For the Asuras were indeed defeated.
9.5.1.[18] Now, that which is the Truth—that is the threefold knowledge. Those gods said, "Having performed the sacrifice, let us extend this Truth."
They performed the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering. Now, the Asuras became aware of this: "The gods, having indeed prepared the sacrifice..."
"Go forth! We shall fetch that which is ours from there," they said, and having thus performed the *samiṣṭayajus* offering, they departed.

Therefore, they do not perform the *samiṣṭayajus* for that sacrifice. When the gods saw the Asuras, they snatched away the sacrifice and resolved to perform something else, thinking, "They are indeed doing something different."
Again they departed (9.5.1.20). When they had departed, he offered the Prāyaṇīya [oblation]; the Asuras indeed perceived that very act of his.

"Recite the *śamyor* [verse]; sit down; you have come. Therefore, that sacrifice is called *śamyuvant*. When those gods saw the Asuras, they snatched up the sacrifice and resolved to perform something else entirely. "They are doing something different," they thought, and so they departed once more. (9.5.1) When they had departed...

Having purchased and led away the King (Soma), they then prepared the guest-offering for him; but the Asuras became aware of this very act. When the *iḍā* had been invoked, they arrived. Therefore, that sacrifice ends with the *iḍā*. Seeing the Asuras, the gods snatched up the sacrifice and resolved to perform something else entirely, thinking, "They are doing something different."
They died once again. When they had died, they performed the *upasad* rites; having recited only three *sāmidhenī* verses, they sacrificed to the deities alone.
They set aside both the *prayāja*s and the *anuyāja*s from the sacrifice, for they were most hurried there;

therefore, at the *upasads*, having recited only three *sāmidhenī* verses, he sacrifices to the deities alone, and does not set aside either the *prayāja*s or the *anuyāja*s from the sacrifice. 9.5.1. [23]
On the day of preparation, they immolated the animal victim for Agni and Soma.
The Asuras became aware of this very act; they arrived while his *samiṣṭayajus* offerings had not yet been offered. Therefore, one does not offer the *samiṣṭayajus* for that animal victim.
Those gods [conquered] the Asuras;
when they had departed, they performed the morning pressing every morning, and the Asuras indeed became aware of that.
They did for him as much as was required until the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*). Then those gods went forth against the Asuras;
when they had departed, they performed the midday libation (*mādhyandinaṃ savanam*), and the Asuras indeed perceived that very act.

He did for him only this much, until the midday [pressing]. Then those gods went against the Asuras. When they had departed, they proceeded with the animal sacrifice of the *savanīya* offering; the Asuras indeed perceived that very act.

They performed for him as much as is performed for this animal sacrifice. Then those gods came against the Asuras; when they had departed, they performed the third pressing and completed it. That which they completed was everything.

Then the Asuras, failing to attain the truth, were scattered; then the gods prevailed, while the Asuras were defeated. He who knows this prevails by himself, and his hateful rival is defeated. 9.5.1. [28] Those gods said:

"These sacrifices which have been completed with material offerings—know how we may bring those which we have left behind to completion. They said, "Meditate! By this they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)! "Seek it so that we may bring these sacrifices to completion. 9.5.1. [29]

While reflecting, they saw these *samiṣṭayajus* offerings; they offered them, and by means of them they completed these sacrifices. Because they completed (*saṃsthāpayan*) them, they are called *saṃsthitayajūṃṣi*; and because they sacrificed together (*samayajan*), they are called *samiṣṭayajūṃṣi*. 9.5.1 [30]
Now, these indeed are the nine sacrifices;
these are the nine *samiṣṭayajus* offerings.
In that he offers these, he thereby brings those very sacrifices to completion. He offers both: those of the *adhvara* sacrifice and those of the fire-sacrifice (*agni*). Of the *adhvara*...
The connection for the former [offerings] of that fire has been stated.
He offers two oblations to Agni;
the sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni—as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure.
By that much alone he completes this sacrifice [with the formula]: "The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus; may Agni, being invoked, fulfill us.
These two sets together amount to eleven;
the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and it is vigor.
By this, he indeed perfects the sacrifice with the power of the *triṣṭubh*.
And as to why there are eleven [stomas]:
the *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables; Indra is connected to the *triṣṭubh*; Indra is the self of the sacrifice; Indra is the sacrifice.
The deity is that very deity who is the self of the sacrifice; in her alone he thus finally establishes this sacrifice.
Having offered the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations, they go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
From the purificatory bath they emerge with the *udayanīya* offering.

Having performed the animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa) of the Anūbandhya sacrifice, he offers the oblations for the Devikās. 9.5.1. [35] Prajāpati, having attained this, indeed considered himself successful; having established himself in the quarters, he [created] all this.
Because he stood supporting and bestowing as he supported and bestowed, therefore he is called Dhātṛ (the Ordainer).
In the same way, the sacrificer, having established himself in the quarters, stands supporting and bestowing all this.
Furthermore, as to why he offers these oblations:

These quarters are this fire; those very same [quarters] he places as those [bricks] in front—the bunch of darbha grass and the loṣṭeṣṭakās. Those are the prāṇabhṛts in the first layer; the entire second layer, the entire third, and the entire fourth. Then, for the fifth layer, there are the asapatnās, the nākasads, and the pañcacūḍās; those are the upward ones.
As they were departing and going away, Prajāpati was afraid of them, thinking, "Alas, all this world will pass beyond these [creatures] as they move away.
Becoming Dhātṛ (the Ordainer), he went around them and established himself within them.
That which is Dhātṛ is yonder Āditya (the Sun).
Now, that which is the supreme stride of the quarters is this very thing upon which he stands while shining.
He who is that Creator (Dhātṛ) is indeed this Dhātra.

There is a cake on twelve potsherds; the cake is on twelve potsherds because the year has twelve months, the year is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is Dhātṛ. Now, as for that highest stride of the quarters, these are those former oblations: a pap for Anumati, a pap for Rākā, and a pap for Sinīvālī.
The *caru* for Kuhū: when he offers these [oblations], he thereby establishes him in that which is the furthest reach of the quarters. He offers it all; this is for the sake of its completeness.
These, indeed, are the goddesses.

For these quarters are indeed the *chandas*, and the *chandas* are goddesses; and this "Ka" is Prajāpati. Because they are both the goddesses and Ka, there are five Devikā offerings, for there are five quarters.
Regarding this, they say: "One should not offer these oblations, lest one should cause an excess. However, one should indeed offer them, for they are for the sake of desires.

These oblations are offered; indeed, there is nothing in excess of desires. Whatever oblation is offered subsequent to the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), that very sacrificial essence (*medhas*) is placed in the midst of the animal itself. He offers both types: those of the *adhvara* sacrifice and those of Agni.
First those of the *adhvara*, then those of Agni; the significance of this has already been explained. [The latter are] in a loud voice.

There is an animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa) performed in a low voice, for this is indeed an iṣṭi sacrifice. [The formulas are: "Recite the invitatory verse," "Prompt the priest," and for the animal-cake offering, "Recite the invitatory verse," "Offer the oblation. For these, the sviṣṭakṛt offering is the same, and the iḍā portion is the same. 9.5.1. [41] Now, regarding this very animal sacrifice:
They offer the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations and descend for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*),
for this animal sacrifice is concluded by means of the heart-spike. Having performed the rite with the heart-spike and returned, he offers the oblations to Viśvakarman.

"All works"—these are all the works performed here by this Agni; he gratifies them with this [offering] and makes them a deity with the oblation. For that deity for whom an oblation is taken is indeed a deity, but not that one for whom it is not taken; and furthermore—

This Agni is Viśvakarman; it is him he thus gratifies. Furthermore, as to why he offers the Vaiśvakarmaṇa oblations: the Sāvitra oblations are both the beginning and the rising of Agni, while the Vaiśvakarmaṇas are the beginning.

The *vaiśvakarman* offerings constitute the "rising. If he were to offer only the *sāvitra* oblations and not the *vaiśvakarman* ones, it would be as if he performed the "starting" (the descent) but not the "rising"; such would that be. But if he were to offer only the *vaiśvakarman* oblations and not the *sāvitra* ones, it would be as if he performed the "rising" but not the "starting"; such would that be. Therefore, he offers both: the starting and the rising.
It effects that rising;
there are eight Vasus.
Thus, just as the departure [was performed], so does one effect the rising with the utterance of "svāhā."

For those [sacrifices], the ninth [offering] occurs; thus he makes their rising just as their departure was. For those [sacrifices], the tenth [offering] occurs; thus he makes their rising just as their departure was. There he offers a continuous oblation; for there the sacrifice is indeed seed, so as not to interrupt the seed. Here, however, he offers with the *sruva* ladle.

For the *svāhā*-utterance is indeed the manifest seed once it has been born. (9.5.1.45) "Whatever flowed together from intention, or from the heart, or was gathered from the mind, or from the eye"—from all this, indeed, the ritual action (*karman*) first came into being. Follow after that to the world of those who have performed good deeds.
"Wherein the ancient seers, the first-born, went"—by this he refers to these very seers.
"This common dwelling-place, I bestow upon you"—the world of heaven is indeed the common dwelling-place; thus he [bestows him] for the sake of the heavenly world.
"Jātavedas bestows that treasure which he has brought; the lord of the sacrifice shall follow you here. Recognize him in the highest heaven!"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
"Know this one. 9.5.1 [47]

"In the highest heaven, O gods, dwelling together, know his form when he has come by the paths traveled by the gods; may you make our sacrifices and pious works manifest. As the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*). "Awake, O Agni, with that [power] wherewith thou carriest [the offerings]"—the significance of these two is their color. 9.5.1 [48]

"By means of the sacrificial grass-mat, the enclosing sticks, the ladle, the altar, and the sacrificial straw—by means of these forms of our sacrifice, lead this sacrifice of ours to heaven among the gods; that is to say, 'cause us to go to the heavenly world by means of these forms of the sacrifice. 9.5.1 [49]

"What has been given, what has been received from others, what has been offered as a pūrtam, and whatever sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) there are— may Agni Vaiśvakarman place that among the gods in heaven for us. Thus, both what one gives at the present moment and what one gives not at the present moment, may he grant that to us.
"May Agni Vaiśvakarman place this in the heavenly world"— this means:
"Where the streams of honey and of clarified butter do not fail, there may Agni Vaiśvakarman place us among the gods in heaven."
"He bears"—the significance of this is exactly as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) itself states.
9.5.1 [51]. He offers eight oblations to Viśvakarman.
The *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of the *gāyatrī* nature; as great as Agni is, as great as his...
By this much food, he thus gratifies him.
Having offered the Vaiśvakarman oblations, he gives him a name;
for when one has been born entirely and completely, then indeed one receives a name.
For here indeed this entire whole is born.
Having performed the naming, he then worships it;
for with his entire self he builds him up.

If one were not to utter this self-consecration here, then indeed he would exclude his own self from it; but since he utters this self-consecration here, he does not exclude his own self from it: "Thou art the highest of those fires belonging to the five peoples who are upon this earth; impel us toward life. Whosoever...

"The five-layered fires are upon this earth; of these, you are the best. Impel us forward toward life"—with this *anuṣṭubh* verse he pays homage. For the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech is all the meters; thus he pays homage to him with all the meters.
Having paid homage and having caused the fire to ascend [into himself], he departs.
Having churned [the fire], he performs the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice.
Then he sacrifices with the curd-mixture (*payasyā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
He who performs this rite indeed becomes one among the gods.

The divine pair is Mitra and Varuṇa. If he were to approach a human woman without having sacrificed with this [offering], that would be a descent; it would be as if one who is divine were to become human. But when he sacrifices with this curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa, he approaches that very divine pair; having sacrificed with this, he may [then] act according to his desire.
One should act in a manner that is appropriate.
Furthermore, as for why he sacrifices with this curd-mixture dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa:
when Prajāpati had become relaxed, his semen fell away.
Where the gods restored him, they placed seed in him by means of this curdled milk offering to Mitra and Varuṇa;
in the same way, this sacrificer now places it in him. 9.5.1.
[56] Now, he who was that Prajāpati became relaxed.

This very one is he who is built as the fire-altar; and that seed which fell away from him is this curd-offering (payasyā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing, and it is out-breathing and in-breathing that transform the emitted seed. It is a curd-offering because seed is milk; thus the sacrifice becomes [the seed].
For the sacrifice is indeed the seed of the sacrifice; it takes place in a whisper, for seed is poured out in a whisper; it takes place at the end, for seed is deposited at the end.
They proceed with its whey.

In that case, he bestows the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). "One should give a pair of hornless [heifers]," so they say; but Māhitthi said, "I think it is merely by way of a formal injunction. Indeed, this offering made upon what is not a brick is a leaking offering for one who has piled the fire-altar;
it is an offering of Soma. 9.5.1. [58]
He should lay down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks themselves.
These worlds indeed are the *svayamātṛṇṇā*s; these worlds are this piled fire-altar.
He should also lay down the seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks.
The seasonal bricks are indeed the year; this built-up fire-altar is the year. One should lay down the Viśvajyotis bricks;
these deities are indeed the Viśvajyotis, and these deities are this built-up fire-altar.
Furthermore, he should lay down the *cit* itself;
for this is indeed a renewed sacrifice, and this is a subsequent worship of the gods.
Thus, he lays down a renewed sacrifice and a subsequent worship of the gods; verily, the renewed sacrifice does not fail him.
One should act in such a way that whatever fire is deposited upon the altar, this entire fire becomes that very brick.
Thus, when one offers oblations into the fire, it is as if these oblations of his have been offered into the entire *cāṇḍila* fire when it has been built up with wings and tail. 9.5.1. [62]

Indeed, all beings and all the gods become embryos for him who maintains the fire. He who piles the fire-altar without having maintained it for a full year brings forth these very beings as an embryo that has been born; indeed, he who [does so]...
"It destroys a human embryo; that indeed is what they point out. But as for this [other one], it is divine.

One should not be the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) for one who has not carried it for a year," so said Vātsya. "Lest I incur guilt by performing the sacrifice for one whose seed is divine when it is being destroyed. 9.5.1. [63]
"One should pile [the fire-altar] for at most six months," they say;
"for embryos born after six months are living.
If he were to recite the Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*) before the year-long maintenance [of the fire], he should recite the eighties of verses (*ṛcaśītī*); for that is incomplete.
In that he has not been maintained for a year, that is incomplete; and in that there are *ṛk-aśītis*, he would draw him out even further.
Whether he has been maintained for a year or not maintained for a year, he should recite the entire Great Litany (*mahaduktha*). 9.5.1 [64]

Then Śāṇḍilyāyana went toward the East. Daivyampāti said to him, "Śāṇḍilyāyana, how is the fire-altar to be built? We are weary; we desire to build the fire-altar after it has been carried for a year. 9.5.1 [65]
He said: "One may indeed build it at will, provided that he has previously maintained it for a year; for it is only when it has been thus maintained that one builds it. 9.5.1.
[66] One may indeed build it at will.
He who intends to press [Soma] for a year— verily, this [fire-altar] sustains him directly with food through these oblations.
However, he may indeed build it at his own will.
He who offers the Agnihotra for a year indeed carries it;
he who offers the Agnihotra supports it.
However, one may build it [the fire-altar] at will.
He who has been born for a year—Agni is indeed breath—and it is that [breath] which sustains him. Now, when seed is emitted, the breath descends after it;
he finds it, and because he finds whatever is born as it is born, he is called Jātavedas. Therefore, one who knows this may, if he so desires, pile the fire-altar immediately after its birth.

Indeed, when one who knows this drinks or causes [another] to drink, those very offerings of his become as if they were offered upon a completely piled fire-altar (agnicayana) provided with wings and tail. 9.5.2. Indra perceived this *sarpis-ṛca* for the fulfillment of what is deficient, for the removal of what is redundant, and for the perfection of what is unsuccessful. And then...
Or if a man, having piled the fire-altar, should encounter some misfortune or stumble, when Śyāparṇa Sāyakāyana heard this, he then undertook this rite.
This is the perfection of the triad.
The prosperity of Agni belongs to him who piles the fire; the prosperity belongs to him who piles the fire. 9.5.2.
[3] Now, as to why he worships with this [verse]: it is for the sake of that prosperity.

Whatever he here either knows or does not know, whether he recites it or does not cause it to be studied, all that becomes attained for him by this [rite], including whatever of his remains unattained; and whatever desire there is in that *anuṣṭubh* verse, even that he attains right here; furthermore, from this very ritual act, he drives away the *rakṣases* and the destroyers.
They listen to this man as he speaks; therefore, one who knows this may at will pile the fire-altar for another, for he is capable of becoming superior.
9.5.2 [4] For the slaying of Vṛtra, for strength.

With the two verses beginning with "sahadānum puruhūta kṣiyantam," he worships with the first two [verses] addressed to Vṛtrahan. For indeed, having slain Vṛtra—the evil—having been freed from evil, the gods performed this rite; in the very same way, the sacrificer [performs it] after slaying Vṛtra—the evil.

"Having slain [the enemy], he, whose evil has been struck away, performs this rite. With the two verses addressed to the Dispeller of Enemies (*vaimṛdhī*), [he recites]: "O Indra, strike down our adversaries; like a fearsome wild beast that wanders and dwells in the mountains... 9.5.2.[5]
By means of these two [verses], the gods, having struck down their adversaries and evil, performed this rite as those whose evil had been struck away;
in the very same way, the sacrificer, having struck down his adversaries and evil, performs this rite as one whose evil has been struck away.
"Vaiśvānara for our aid... (RV 3.26.1).
"Agni is asked in heaven, Agni is asked on earth"— with these two third verses addressed to Vaiśvānara, the gods, having burnt away evil by means of Vaiśvānara and being freed from evil,
performed this rite; in the very same way, the sacrificer [performs it] by means of Vaiśvānara, [burning away his evil].
Having burned [the body], he, with his evil removed, performs this rite:
"O Agni, through your protection, may we attain our desire.
With this single verse containing the word "desire" (kāma), the gods [performed it].
Having struck away evil with one verse containing a wish, they finally made all desires their own in a single way.
In the same way, the sacrificer, having struck away evil with the six-verse hymn, finally makes all desires his own in a single way with one verse containing a wish. 9.5.2. [8]
It consists of seven verses.
The fire-altar has seven layers; there are seven seasons, seven directions, seven worlds of the gods, seven *stomas*, seven *pṛṣṭhas*, seven meters, seven domestic animals, and seven wild animals.
The vital breaths in the head—whatever constitutes the sevenfold [hymn] with respect to the deities and with respect to the self—one thereby obtains all that.
These [breaths] culminate in the *anuṣṭubh*; for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech. By means of speech, one thereby obtains whatever of his has not yet been obtained. 9.5.2. [9]
"One should worship with an eight-verse hymn," so some say;

[using] the second verse, "For we have granted your desire today," which contains the word *kāma* (desire), together with the seven preceding ones—that makes eight; for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is...

"By that much alone he obtains whatever of his was not yet obtained; thus the two deities share equally. One should not do so. These indeed become seven or eight *anuṣṭubh*s. Whatever desire there is in the eight-verse hymn, one obtains that right here. 9.5.2. [10]
He worships with verses addressed to Indra and Agni.

Since the fire-altar belongs to Indra and Agni, as great as the fire is, as great as its measure is, so much of it does he thereby obtain—whatever of it was previously unobtained. Indeed, Indra and Agni are all the gods; thus it belongs to all the deities.

"As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by just that much he obtains whatever of his remains unobtained. Regarding this, some perform this introductory verse for every single ritual act, thinking, "Let us perform this rite with our evil dispelled. Others say, "One should worship after having constructed a layer (citi) provided with loose soil (purīṣavatī)," for it is there that [the verse] truly resides.
"It becomes entirely whole; therefore, one may do as one desires. This concludes the section on piling (*cayana*); now follows the section on non-piling (*acayana*). There are indeed three oceans:
Agni is the ocean of the *yajus* formulas, the *Mahāvrata* is the ocean of the *sāman* chants, and the *Mahaduktha* is the ocean of the *ṛc* verses. He who...
He who performs these [rites] for another person dries up those very oceans; as they dry up, his *candāṃsi* (metres) dry up after them;
after the *candāṃsi*, the world; after the world, the self; and after the self, offspring and cattle. Day by day, he who performs these for another becomes more wretched. 9.5.2. [13]
Now, if one should cause someone else to sacrifice with all other sacrificial rites without performing these [rites],
his meters are replenished from these very oceans; following the meters comes the world, following the world comes the self, and following the self comes the self.
Offspring and cattle—verily, he becomes better day by day who does not perform these for another.
For this is his divine, immortal self; he who performs these for another gives away that divine self of his to another, and only a withered stump remains. 9.5.2. [14]
Regarding this, some say: "Having done it, they do it again, or they have it done; this is the expiation. One should not do it thus.
It would be as if one were to sprinkle water upon a dry stump; it would either rot or wither away. There is no expiation for this; one should know this. 9.5.2. [15]

Now, Śāṇḍilya used to say: "Tura Kāvaṣeya built a fire-altar for the gods at Kārotyā. The gods asked him: 'O sage, since they say that the building of a fire-altar does not lead to the world of heaven, why then have you built it? 9.5.2. [16]
He said: "What indeed is conducive to the worlds, and what is not? The sacrificer is indeed the self of the sacrifice, and the officiating priests are its limbs.

Where the self is, there are the limbs; where the limbs are, there is the self. If the officiating priests are without worlds, then the sacrificer is likewise without a world, for both become sharers of the same world. However, one should not bargain over the sacrificial fees."
"By means of agreement alone, the officiating priests [attain] the worlds."
